sets.title: Directional terms on a body outline

labels.name: Superior
labels.fn: Toward the head, or above another part. In anatomical position your chest is superior to your abdomen.

follow.q: In anatomical position, which statement uses "superior" correctly?
options: The nose is superior to the mouth
The knee is superior to the hip
The hand is superior to the elbow
The feet are superior to the knees
follow.why: Superior means closer to the head. The nose sits above the mouth. The knee lies below the hip, the hand below the elbow (arms hang at the sides), and the feet below the knees.

labels.name: Right
labels.fn: The body's own right side: the subject's right, not yours. In a front view the subject's right appears on your left, which is why figures label it.

follow.q: You face a patient standing in anatomical position. On which side of your view is the patient's left arm?
options: It depends on which way the palms face
follow.why: Directional terms always use the patient's own left and right. Facing someone, their left arm is on your right, just as in a front-view figure.

labels.name: Left
labels.fn: The body's own left side: the subject's left, not yours. In a front view the subject's left appears on your right.

labels.name: Cranial
labels.fn: Toward the head end of the body; used much like superior. It comes from the Latin word for the skull.

labels.name: Proximal
labels.fn: On a limb, closer to where it attaches to the trunk. The elbow is proximal to the wrist; the knee is proximal to the ankle.

follow.q: Which statement uses "proximal" correctly?
options: The elbow is proximal to the wrist
The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The ankle is proximal to the knee
The fingers are proximal to the palm
follow.why: Proximal is measured along a limb from where it joins the trunk. The elbow is nearer the shoulder than the wrist is, so the elbow is proximal. The other three reverse the order.

labels.name: Posterior or dorsal
labels.fn: Toward the back of the body. Your spine and heels are on the posterior side. Dorsal (from dorsum, the back) means the same thing in an upright person.

labels.name: Anterior or ventral
labels.fn: Toward the front of the body. Your nose and toes are on the anterior side. Ventral (belly side) means the same thing in a person standing upright.

follow.q: Which pair of terms means the same thing in a person standing in anatomical position?
follow.why: Ventral means the belly side, and in an upright person the belly faces forward, so ventral and anterior coincide. Dorsal is the back, caudal is toward the tail, and medial and lateral are opposites.

labels.name: Medial
labels.fn: Toward the midline, the imaginary line down the center of the body. In anatomical position your little finger is medial to your thumb.

follow.q: In anatomical position, where is the thumb compared with the little finger?
follow.why: In anatomical position the palms face forward, so the thumb is on the outer side of the hand, farther from the midline. Farther from the midline is lateral; the little finger is medial.

labels.name: Lateral
labels.fn: Away from the midline, toward the side. In anatomical position your ears are lateral to your eyes.

labels.name: Caudal
labels.fn: Toward the tail end, the bottom of the trunk; used much like inferior. It comes from cauda, Latin for tail.

labels.name: Proximal
labels.fn: On a limb, closer to where it attaches to the trunk. The elbow is proximal to the wrist; the knee is proximal to the ankle.

follow.q: Which statement uses "proximal" correctly?
options: The elbow is proximal to the wrist
The wrist is proximal to the elbow
The ankle is proximal to the knee
The fingers are proximal to the palm
follow.why: Proximal is measured along a limb from where it joins the trunk. The elbow is nearer the shoulder than the wrist is, so the elbow is proximal. The other three reverse the order.

labels.name: Distal
labels.fn: On a limb, farther from where it attaches to the trunk. The fingers are distal to the wrist; the toes are distal to the ankle.

labels.name: Distal
labels.fn: On a limb, farther from where it attaches to the trunk. The fingers are distal to the wrist; the toes are distal to the ankle.

labels.name: Inferior
labels.fn: Away from the head, or below another part. In anatomical position your knees are inferior to your hips.

labels.name: Sagittal plane
labels.fn: A vertical plane that divides the body into left and right parts. Down the exact middle it is the midsagittal plane, making equal halves; off center it is a parasagittal plane.

follow.q: A cut divides the brain into left and right halves. Which plane is it?
follow.why: A plane that separates left from right is sagittal, and one down the exact middle is midsagittal. A frontal plane separates front from back, and a transverse plane separates top from bottom.

labels.name: Frontal (coronal) plane
labels.fn: A vertical plane that divides the body into front (anterior) and back (posterior) parts. It is also called the coronal plane.

follow.q: Which plane separates the anterior part of the body from the posterior part?
follow.why: The frontal plane runs side to side and top to bottom, like a wall you face, so it splits front from back. Sagittal planes split left from right, and transverse planes split top from bottom.

labels.name: Transverse plane
labels.fn: A horizontal plane that divides the body into upper (superior) and lower (inferior) parts. A slice along it is a cross section, the view in most CT scans.

follow.q: A CT scan shows a slice through the abdomen as if you were looking up from the feet. Which plane is the slice in?
follow.why: A slice that shows the body in cross section, separating upper from lower, lies in the transverse (horizontal) plane. CT images are usually displayed that way, viewed from below.

labels.name: Oblique plane
labels.fn: Any plane cut at an angle between the three standard planes. Oblique sections are harder to read because structures appear stretched or tilted.

labels.name: Cranial cavity
labels.fn: The part of the dorsal body cavity inside the skull. It holds the brain.

labels.name: Cranial cavity
labels.fn: The part of the dorsal body cavity inside the skull. It holds the brain.

labels.name: Vertebral cavity
labels.fn: The part of the dorsal body cavity that runs down the back inside the spine. It holds the spinal cord and is continuous with the cranial cavity.

follow.q: The brain and the spinal cord sit in which body cavity?
follow.why: The dorsal body cavity is the one continuous space made of the cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral cavity (spinal cord). The ventral cavity, with the thoracic cavity and mediastinum inside it, holds the organs of the trunk.

labels.name: Thoracic cavity
labels.fn: The upper part of the ventral body cavity, above the diaphragm. It holds the two pleural cavities with the lungs and, between them, the mediastinum with the heart.

labels.name: Superior mediastinum
labels.fn: The upper part of the mediastinum, above the heart. It holds the large vessels at the top of the heart, the trachea, the esophagus and the thymus.

labels.name: Dorsal body cavity
labels.fn: The cavity toward the back of the body. It holds the brain and spinal cord and has two parts: the cranial cavity and the vertebral cavity.

labels.name: Pleural cavity
labels.fn: The thin space around each lung between two layers of serous membrane. Serous fluid in it lets the lung slide against the chest wall as you breathe.

follow.q: What lies directly between the two pleural cavities?
follow.why: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity, between the two lungs' pleural cavities. It contains the heart in its own pericardial cavity plus the other midline organs. The diaphragm lies below all of them.

labels.name: Pericardial cavity within the mediastinum
labels.fn: The thin, fluid-filled space around the heart, between two layers of serous membrane. It sits inside the mediastinum.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Vertebral cavity
labels.fn: The part of the dorsal body cavity that runs down the back inside the spine. It holds the spinal cord and is continuous with the cranial cavity.

follow.q: The brain and the spinal cord sit in which body cavity?
follow.why: The dorsal body cavity is the one continuous space made of the cranial cavity (brain) and the vertebral cavity (spinal cord). The ventral cavity, with the thoracic cavity and mediastinum inside it, holds the organs of the trunk.

labels.name: Ventral body cavity
labels.fn: The large cavity at the front of the trunk. The diaphragm divides it into the thoracic cavity above and the abdominopelvic cavity below.

labels.name: Abdominal cavity
labels.fn: The upper part of the abdominopelvic cavity. It holds the stomach, liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas, kidneys and most of the intestines.

labels.name: Abdominopelvic cavity
labels.fn: The lower part of the ventral body cavity, below the diaphragm. It has no wall inside it, but is described as an upper abdominal cavity and a lower pelvic cavity.

labels.name: Pelvic cavity
labels.fn: The lower part of the abdominopelvic cavity, inside the bony pelvis. It holds the urinary bladder, the end of the intestine and the internal reproductive organs.

labels.name: Pericardial cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the two layers of the serous membrane around the heart. In the comparison it is the air inside the balloon: a closed sac that the heart pushes into without ever entering it.

labels.name: Frons
labels.fn: The forehead. Its adjective is frontal.

labels.name: Oculus
labels.fn: The eye. Its adjective is orbital or ocular.

labels.name: Bucca
labels.fn: The cheek. Its adjective is buccal, as in a buccal swab from inside the cheek.

labels.name: Auris
labels.fn: The ear. Its adjective is otic.

labels.name: Facies
labels.fn: The face. Its adjective is facial.

labels.name: Nasus
labels.fn: The nose. Its adjective is nasal.

labels.name: Cervicis
labels.fn: The neck. Its adjective is cervical, so the cervical region is the neck.

follow.q: A "cervical" injury is an injury to which region?
follow.why: Cervicis means neck, so its adjective, cervical, refers to the neck region. The chest is thoracic, the lower back lumbar, and the wrist carpal.

labels.name: Oris
labels.fn: The mouth. Its adjective is oral.

labels.name: Mentis
labels.fn: The chin. Its adjective is mental (from mentum, chin), not to be confused with the mind.

labels.name: Thoracis or thorax
labels.fn: The chest. Its adjective is thoracic.

labels.name: Axilla
labels.fn: The armpit. Its adjective is axillary.

labels.name: Mamma
labels.fn: The breast. Its adjective is mammary.

labels.name: Brachium
labels.fn: The arm in the strict anatomical sense: only the part between the shoulder and the elbow. Its adjective is brachial.

follow.q: In anatomical terms, the "brachium" is which part of the upper limb?
options: Between the shoulder and the elbow
Between the elbow and the wrist
The whole limb from shoulder to fingers
follow.why: Anatomy uses "arm" (brachium) only for the segment from shoulder to elbow. From elbow to wrist is the forearm (antebrachium: ante means before), and the hand is the manus.

labels.name: Trunk
labels.fn: The body apart from the head, neck and limbs: the thorax, abdomen and pelvis together.

labels.name: Abdomen
labels.fn: The belly, between the thorax and the pelvis. Its adjective is abdominal.

labels.name: Antecubitis
labels.fn: The front of the elbow. Its adjective is antecubital; the antecubital area is where blood is most often drawn.

labels.name: Umbilicus
labels.fn: The navel. Its adjective is umbilical; the umbilical region is the central abdomen around it.

labels.name: Antebrachium
labels.fn: The forearm, between the elbow and the wrist. Ante- means before or in front of: it is the fore-arm, the part of the limb just beyond the brachium, the arm. Its adjective is antebrachial.

labels.name: Hip
labels.fn: The region where the thigh joins the trunk, on each side. Its adjective is coxal.

labels.name: Carpus
labels.fn: The wrist. Its adjective is carpal.

labels.name: Pelvis
labels.fn: The lowest part of the trunk, below the abdomen. Its adjective is pelvic.

labels.name: Palma
labels.fn: The palm of the hand. Its adjective is palmar.

labels.name: Inguen
labels.fn: The groin, where the thigh meets the front of the trunk. Its adjective is inguinal.

labels.name: Crus
labels.fn: The leg in the strict anatomical sense: only the part between the knee and the ankle. Its adjective is crural.

labels.name: Tarsus
labels.fn: The ankle. Its adjective is tarsal.

labels.name: Pes
labels.fn: The foot. Its adjective is pedal, as in the pedal pulse on top of the foot.

labels.name: Cephalon
labels.fn: The head. Its adjective is cephalic.

labels.name: Shoulder
labels.fn: The region where the upper limb joins the trunk. Its adjective is acromial.

labels.name: Cervicis
labels.fn: The neck. Its adjective is cervical, so the cervical region is the neck.

follow.q: A "cervical" injury is an injury to which region?
follow.why: Cervicis means neck, so its adjective, cervical, refers to the neck region. The chest is thoracic, the lower back lumbar, and the wrist carpal.

labels.name: Dorsum
labels.fn: The back. Its adjective is dorsal.

labels.name: Brachium
labels.fn: The arm in the strict anatomical sense: only the part between the shoulder and the elbow. Its adjective is brachial.

follow.q: In anatomical terms, the "brachium" is which part of the upper limb?
options: Between the shoulder and the elbow
Between the elbow and the wrist
The whole limb from shoulder to fingers
follow.why: Anatomy uses "arm" (brachium) only for the segment from shoulder to elbow. From elbow to wrist is the forearm (antebrachium: ante means before), and the hand is the manus.

labels.name: Lumbus
labels.fn: The lower back, between the thorax and the pelvis. Its adjective is lumbar.

labels.name: Upper limb
labels.fn: The whole limb from the shoulder to the fingers: arm (brachium), forearm (antebrachium), wrist (carpus) and hand (manus).

labels.name: Antebrachium
labels.fn: The forearm, between the elbow and the wrist. Ante- means before or in front of: it is the fore-arm, the part of the limb just beyond the brachium, the arm. Its adjective is antebrachial.

labels.name: Manus
labels.fn: The hand. Its adjective is manual.

labels.name: Gluteus
labels.fn: The buttock. Its adjective is gluteal.

labels.name: Lower limb
labels.fn: The whole limb from the hip to the toes: thigh, leg (crus), ankle (tarsus) and foot (pes).

labels.name: Popliteus
labels.fn: The back of the knee. Its adjective is popliteal.

labels.name: Sura
labels.fn: The calf, the back of the leg. Its adjective is sural.

labels.name: Planta
labels.fn: The sole of the foot. Its adjective is plantar.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Right hypochondriac region
labels.fn: The upper right of the nine abdominal regions, under the lower edge of the ribcage (hypo- under, chondr- gristle, for the gristly lower edge of the ribcage). Most of the liver and the gallbladder lie here.

labels.name: Epigastric region
labels.fn: The upper middle of the nine abdominal regions, over the stomach (epi- upon, gastr- stomach). Much of the stomach and part of the liver lie here.

follow.q: A patient points to pain just below the tip of the breastbone, in the middle. Which region is that?
follow.why: The upper middle of the nine-region grid is the epigastric region. The umbilical region is the center around the navel, the hypogastric region is the lower middle, and the hypochondriac regions are the upper sides.

labels.name: Left hypochondriac region
labels.fn: The upper left of the nine abdominal regions, under the lower edge of the ribcage. Part of the stomach and the spleen lie here.

labels.name: Right lumbar region
labels.fn: The middle right of the nine abdominal regions, at the level of the lower back (lumbus).

labels.name: Umbilical region
labels.fn: The central of the nine abdominal regions, around the navel.

labels.name: Left lumbar region
labels.fn: The middle left of the nine abdominal regions, at the level of the lower back (lumbus).

labels.name: Right iliac region
labels.fn: The lower right of the nine abdominal regions, beside the bony ridge of the hip. The appendix is usually here. Also called the right inguinal region.

labels.name: Hypogastric region
labels.fn: The lower middle of the nine abdominal regions, below the navel. The urinary bladder lies here; it is also called the pubic region.

labels.name: Left iliac region
labels.fn: The lower left of the nine abdominal regions, beside the bony ridge of the hip. Also called the left inguinal region.

labels.name: Right upper quadrant (RUQ)
labels.fn: The upper right of the four abdominal quadrants, formed by a vertical and a horizontal line through the navel. It holds most of the liver and the gallbladder.

follow.q: Pain from an inflamed gallbladder is felt mainly in which quadrant?
follow.why: The liver fills most of the upper right abdomen, and the gallbladder sits under it, so gallbladder pain centers in the right upper quadrant. The appendix is usually in the right lower quadrant, and the spleen in the left upper.

labels.name: Left upper quadrant (LUQ)
labels.fn: The upper left of the four abdominal quadrants. It holds most of the stomach and the spleen.

labels.name: Right lower quadrant (RLQ)
labels.fn: The lower right of the four abdominal quadrants. The appendix is usually here, so appendicitis pain settles in this quadrant.

labels.name: Left lower quadrant (LLQ)
labels.fn: The lower left of the four abdominal quadrants, holding coils of the intestine.

labels.name: Glycoprotein
labels.fn: A membrane protein with a sugar chain attached on the outside. Together with glycolipids it forms the glycocalyx, the sugar coat that marks the cell's identity.

labels.name: Glycolipid
labels.fn: A lipid in the outer layer of the membrane with a sugar chain attached. It is part of the glycocalyx, the sugar coat on the cell's outer surface.

labels.name: Peripheral membrane protein
labels.fn: A protein attached loosely to one face of the membrane, usually to an integral protein, rather than set into the bilayer. Many are enzymes or anchor the cell's internal framework.

labels.name: Phospholipid bilayer
labels.fn: The two-layer sheet of phospholipids that forms the membrane. Their water-loving heads face the fluid on both sides and their water-fearing tails face each other, so ions and water-soluble molecules cannot pass straight through.

follow.q: Why can a small lipid-soluble molecule cross the membrane on its own, but an ion cannot?
options: Its hydrophobic core lets lipid-soluble molecules dissolve through but repels ions
Ions are too large to squeeze through the gaps between neighboring phospholipids
Cholesterol binds ions and holds them outside
follow.why: The middle of the bilayer is a layer of fatty tails. A molecule that dissolves in lipid can pass through it; a charged ion is surrounded by water and is repelled by that hydrophobic core, so it needs a protein path.

labels.name: Integral membrane protein
labels.fn: A protein that spans the bilayer or is embedded in it. Many act as channels or carriers that let particular substances cross.

labels.name: Cholesterol
labels.fn: A steroid tucked between the phospholipids. It keeps the membrane from becoming too stiff in the cold or too fluid in the heat.

labels.name: Mitochondria
labels.fn: Organelles with a double membrane whose inner membrane is folded into shelves. They make most of the cell's ATP using oxygen, so active cells such as muscle have many.

follow.q: A cell uses a lot of ATP all the time. What would you expect to see in it?
follow.why: Mitochondria make most of a cell's ATP, so cells with a high, steady demand, such as the cells of the heart wall, are packed with them.

labels.name: Intermediate filament
labels.fn: A rope-like cytoskeleton fiber of medium thickness, made of tough fibrous proteins. It resists pulling and holds the cell's shape.

labels.name: Plasma membrane
labels.fn: The boundary of the cell: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins set in it. It controls what enters and leaves the cell.

labels.name: Ribosomes
labels.fn: Small particles, free in the cytosol or stuck to the rough ER, where proteins are built from amino acids.

labels.name: Microtubule
labels.fn: The thickest cytoskeleton fiber: a hollow tube of tubulin. Microtubules act as tracks for moving vesicles and organelles, form the core of cilia, and pull the copied genetic material apart when the cell divides.

labels.name: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
labels.fn: Folded sheets of membrane studded with ribosomes. Proteins made there are threaded inside it to be folded and then sent on to the Golgi apparatus, often for export or for the membrane.

follow.q: What makes rough endoplasmic reticulum look rough?
follow.why: The bumps are ribosomes making proteins that go into the ER. Smooth ER lacks them, and folded inner membranes belong to mitochondria.

labels.name: Centrosome
labels.fn: The region near the nucleus where microtubules are organized. It contains a pair of centrioles and, when the cell divides, organizes the fibers that separate the copied genetic material.

labels.name: Microfilament
labels.fn: The thinnest cytoskeleton fiber, made of actin. Microfilaments let cells change shape and crawl, pinch in two when they divide, and hold up microvilli.

labels.name: Lysosome
labels.fn: A membrane sac full of digestive enzymes that work best in acid. It breaks down worn-out organelles, taken-in particles and large molecules so their parts can be reused.

labels.name: Golgi apparatus
labels.fn: A stack of flattened membrane sacs that receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies and sorts them, and ships them out in vesicles to the membrane, to lysosomes or out of the cell.

follow.q: A protein made for export leaves the rough ER. Where does it go next?
options: To the Golgi apparatus, in a transport vesicle
Straight out of the cell through the membrane
follow.why: Proteins for export travel from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus in transport vesicles. The Golgi finishes and sorts them, then packs them into secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane.

labels.name: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
labels.fn: Tubes of membrane without ribosomes. They make lipids such as phospholipids and steroids, store calcium, and in liver cells help break down drugs and toxins.

labels.name: Secretory vesicle
labels.fn: A membrane bubble that buds from the Golgi apparatus carrying finished product. It fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell.

labels.name: Golgi vesicle
labels.fn: A vesicle budding from the Golgi apparatus, carrying sorted proteins and lipids to their destination.

labels.name: Peroxisome
labels.fn: A small membrane sac with enzymes that break down fatty acids and toxic substances. Its reactions make hydrogen peroxide, which another of its enzymes turns into water and oxygen.

labels.name: Cytoplasm
labels.fn: Everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus: the fluid cytosol and the organelles in it.

labels.name: Vacuole
labels.fn: A membrane-bound space holding fluid or stored material. Human cells have few and small ones.

labels.name: Transport vesicle
labels.fn: A vesicle that carries newly made proteins from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus.

labels.name: Rough ER
labels.fn: Folded sheets of membrane studded with ribosomes. Proteins made there are threaded inside it to be folded and then sent on to the Golgi apparatus, often for export or for the membrane.

follow.q: What makes rough endoplasmic reticulum look rough?
follow.why: The bumps are ribosomes making proteins that go into the ER. Smooth ER lacks them, and folded inner membranes belong to mitochondria.

labels.name: cis face
labels.fn: The receiving side of the Golgi apparatus, facing the ER. Transport vesicles fuse with it and deliver their proteins.

labels.name: Cisternae
labels.fn: The flattened membrane sacs stacked to form the Golgi apparatus. Proteins pass from one to the next and are modified along the way.

labels.name: trans face
labels.fn: The shipping side of the Golgi apparatus, facing the plasma membrane. Finished products bud off it in vesicles.

labels.name: Golgi apparatus
labels.fn: A stack of flattened membrane sacs that receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies and sorts them, and ships them out in vesicles to the membrane, to lysosomes or out of the cell.

follow.q: A protein made for export leaves the rough ER. Where does it go next?
options: To the Golgi apparatus, in a transport vesicle
Straight out of the cell through the membrane
follow.why: Proteins for export travel from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus in transport vesicles. The Golgi finishes and sorts them, then packs them into secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane.

labels.name: Secretory vesicle
labels.fn: A membrane bubble that buds from the Golgi apparatus carrying finished product. It fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell.

labels.name: Plasma membrane
labels.fn: The boundary of the cell: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins set in it. It controls what enters and leaves the cell.

labels.name: trans face
labels.fn: The shipping side of the Golgi apparatus, facing the plasma membrane. Finished products bud off it in vesicles.

labels.name: cis face
labels.fn: The receiving side of the Golgi apparatus, facing the ER. Transport vesicles fuse with it and deliver their proteins.

labels.name: Golgi apparatus
labels.fn: A stack of flattened membrane sacs that receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies and sorts them, and ships them out in vesicles to the membrane, to lysosomes or out of the cell.

follow.q: A protein made for export leaves the rough ER. Where does it go next?
options: To the Golgi apparatus, in a transport vesicle
Straight out of the cell through the membrane
follow.why: Proteins for export travel from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus in transport vesicles. The Golgi finishes and sorts them, then packs them into secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane.

labels.name: Lipid bilayer
labels.fn: The two-layer sheet of phospholipids that forms the membrane. Their water-loving heads face the fluid on both sides and their water-fearing tails face each other, so ions and water-soluble molecules cannot pass straight through.

follow.q: Why can a small lipid-soluble molecule cross the membrane on its own, but an ion cannot?
options: Its hydrophobic core lets lipid-soluble molecules dissolve through but repels ions
Ions are too large to squeeze through the gaps between neighboring phospholipids
Cholesterol binds ions and holds them outside
follow.why: The middle of the bilayer is a layer of fatty tails. A molecule that dissolves in lipid can pass through it; a charged ion is surrounded by water and is repelled by that hydrophobic core, so it needs a protein path.

labels.name: Crystalline core
labels.fn: The dense center drawn here: in many animals a peroxisome holds a crystal of one of its enzymes, but human peroxisomes usually have no such core.

labels.name: Column of tubulin dimers
labels.fn: One of the rows of paired tubulin units that line up side by side to form the wall of a hollow microtubule.

labels.name: Tubulin dimer
labels.fn: The building block of a microtubule: a pair of tubulin proteins. Adding or removing them lets a microtubule grow or shrink quickly.

labels.name: Actin subunit
labels.fn: The building block of a microfilament. Actin units link in two twisted strands; adding and removing them lets the filament grow and shrink.

labels.name: Tight junction
labels.fn: A seal where strands of membrane proteins stitch neighboring cells together near their top. It stops fluid from leaking between the cells, so substances must pass through the cells instead.

follow.q: What is the main job of a tight junction?
options: It seals neighboring cells together so fluid cannot leak between them
It forms open channels that let ions pass directly from one cell to the next
It anchors the cell to the layer beneath it
It spreads pulling forces across a sheet of cells
follow.why: Tight junctions fuse the outer membranes of neighboring cells in a band. Gap junctions pass ions between cells, hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the layer below, and desmosomes spread mechanical stress.

labels.name: Adjacent plasma membranes
labels.fn: The plasma membranes of the two neighboring cells being joined.

labels.name: Strands of transmembrane proteins
labels.fn: The rows of membrane proteins that meet across the tiny gap between cells and zip their membranes together to form a tight junction.

labels.name: Intercellular space
labels.fn: The narrow gap between neighboring cells, filled with extracellular fluid.

labels.name: Gap junction
labels.fn: A cluster of protein channels (connexons) that line up across two neighboring membranes, letting ions and small molecules pass straight from one cell to the next.

follow.q: The cells of the heart wall contract together because electrical signals pass directly from cell to cell. Which junction allows that?
follow.why: Gap junctions are open channels between cells, so ions carrying charge flow from one cell into the next. Tight junctions seal, and desmosomes and hemidesmosomes only anchor.

labels.name: Adjacent plasma membranes
labels.fn: The plasma membranes of the two neighboring cells being joined.

labels.name: Gap between cells
labels.fn: The narrow gap between two cells at a gap junction, bridged by the connexon channels.

labels.name: Connexons
labels.fn: The hollow protein channels of a gap junction. Two connexons, one in each cell's membrane, line up to make a tunnel between the cells.

labels.name: Anchoring junctions
labels.fn: Junctions that fasten cells to each other or to the layer beneath them so a sheet of cells can be stretched without tearing: desmosomes, adherens junctions and hemidesmosomes.

labels.name: Adjacent plasma membranes
labels.fn: The plasma membranes of the two neighboring cells being joined.

labels.name: Plaque
labels.fn: The dense protein pad on the inside of the membrane at an anchoring junction. The linking proteins attach to it on one side and the cytoskeleton on the other.

labels.name: Transmembrane glycoprotein (cadherin)
labels.fn: Cadherins: membrane proteins that reach across the gap and grip the matching proteins of the neighboring cell, holding the two cells together.

labels.name: Intercellular space
labels.fn: The narrow gap between neighboring cells, filled with extracellular fluid.

labels.name: Desmosome
labels.fn: A spot weld between two cells: protein plaques inside each cell, linked across the gap by cadherins and tied to intermediate filaments. It spreads pulling forces through a sheet of cells, as in skin and heart muscle.

labels.name: Adjacent plasma membranes
labels.fn: The plasma membranes of the two neighboring cells being joined.

labels.name: Plaque
labels.fn: The dense protein pad on the inside of the membrane at an anchoring junction. The linking proteins attach to it on one side and the cytoskeleton on the other.

labels.name: Transmembrane glycoprotein (cadherin)
labels.fn: Cadherins: membrane proteins that reach across the gap and grip the matching proteins of the neighboring cell, holding the two cells together.

labels.name: Actin filament
labels.fn: A microfilament made of actin. At an adherens junction it ties the linking proteins to the rest of the cell's cytoskeleton.

labels.name: Intercellular space
labels.fn: The narrow gap between neighboring cells, filled with extracellular fluid.

labels.name: Adherens
labels.fn: An adherens junction: a band of cadherins linking neighboring cells, tied inside each cell to actin microfilaments. It holds cells together and helps a sheet of cells fold.

labels.name: Integrins
labels.fn: Membrane proteins that bind the cell to the material beneath it. At a hemidesmosome they anchor the cell to the layer it sits on.

labels.name: Hemidesmosome
labels.fn: Half of a desmosome: it anchors a cell to the layer beneath it rather than to another cell, using integrins.

labels.name: Nuclear pores
labels.fn: Openings through the nuclear envelope, lined by protein complexes that control which large molecules pass in and out of the nucleus.

follow.q: The nucleolus makes the parts of ribosomes, but ribosomes work in the cytoplasm. How do the parts get there?
options: By dissolving through the lipid of the nuclear envelope
They are released only when the nuclear envelope breaks down
follow.why: Ribosome parts are far too large and water-loving to cross a lipid membrane, and the envelope breaks down only during cell division. Nuclear pores are the controlled gateways through the envelope for large molecules going in or out.

labels.name: Nuclear envelope
labels.fn: The double membrane around the nucleus, continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and pierced by nuclear pores.

labels.name: Chromatin (condensed)
labels.fn: DNA wound around histone proteins. Loose chromatin fills the nucleus between divisions; it condenses into chromosomes before a cell divides.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: The largest organelle, enclosed by a double-membrane envelope. It holds the cell's DNA and controls which proteins the cell makes.

labels.name: Nucleolus
labels.fn: A dense region inside the nucleus, not bounded by a membrane, where the parts of ribosomes are made.

labels.name: Cisternae
labels.fn: The flattened spaces of the rough endoplasmic reticulum, continuous with the space inside the nuclear envelope.

labels.name: Chromosome
labels.fn: One long DNA molecule with its proteins, coiled tightly just before cell division. Human body cells have 46.

labels.name: Histones
labels.fn: Proteins that DNA winds around like thread on a spool. They pack DNA into the nucleus and help control which genes can be read.

labels.name: Chromatin
labels.fn: DNA wound around histone proteins. Loose chromatin fills the nucleus between divisions; it condenses into chromosomes before a cell divides.

labels.name: Nucleosome
labels.fn: One unit of chromatin: a stretch of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histones, like a bead on a string.

labels.name: DNA helix
labels.fn: The DNA molecule itself: two strands twisted around each other, held together by paired bases.

labels.name: Prophase
labels.fn: The first stage of mitosis. Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each two sister chromatids), the nucleolus disappears, and the spindle starts to form.

labels.name: Prometaphase
labels.fn: The stage between prophase and metaphase. The nuclear envelope breaks up and spindle fibers attach to each chromosome.

labels.name: Metaphase
labels.fn: The stage when the chromosomes line up in a single row across the middle of the cell, the metaphase plate.

follow.q: Which event defines metaphase?
options: Chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell
Sister chromatids separate and move to opposite ends
follow.why: Metaphase is the lining-up stage. Chromatids separate in anaphase, new nuclear envelopes form in telophase, and chromatin condenses in prophase.

labels.name: Anaphase
labels.fn: The stage when the sister chromatids of each chromosome split apart and are pulled to opposite ends of the cell.

labels.name: Telophase
labels.fn: The last stage of mitosis. A nuclear envelope forms around each set of chromosomes at the two ends, and the chromosomes loosen back into chromatin.

labels.name: Cytokinesis
labels.fn: Division of the cytoplasm: a ring of actin pinches the cell in two at the cleavage furrow, making two daughter cells. It overlaps the end of mitosis.

shown.why: A bracket naming the whole run of stages, not one stage.

labels.name: Simple squamous epithelium
labels.fn: One layer of flat cells. Being so thin, it lets substances cross easily by diffusion and filtration: it lines the lungs' air sacs, the capillaries (endothelium) and the body cavities (mesothelium).

follow.q: Why is simple squamous epithelium found where substances must diffuse quickly, as in the lungs' air sacs?
options: It is one layer of flat cells, so the diffusion distance is very short
Its cells are covered in microvilli that add surface area for diffusion
It secretes mucus that speeds diffusion
Its many layers protect against friction
follow.why: Diffusion is fastest over short distances. A single layer of very flat cells makes the barrier as thin as possible. Microvilli and mucus belong to columnar epithelia, and many layers would slow diffusion.

labels.name: Stratified squamous epithelium
labels.fn: Many layers of cells, flat at the surface. It resists friction and wear: keratinized in the epidermis of the skin, nonkeratinized in the mouth, esophagus and vagina.

follow.q: Why is the lining of the esophagus stratified rather than simple?
options: Food rubs it, and many layers let worn surface cells be replaced
It must absorb nutrients quickly from the food passing over its surface
It must let gases diffuse through
It must release large amounts of product
follow.why: Stratified squamous epithelium protects against abrasion: the surface cells wear off and new cells from the deep layers replace them. Absorption and diffusion need thin single layers instead.

labels.name: Stratified cuboidal epithelium
labels.fn: Two or more layers of cube-shaped cells. It is uncommon and lines some larger ducts that carry fluids to a surface.

labels.name: Simple cuboidal epithelium
labels.fn: One layer of cube-shaped cells with round central nuclei. It secretes and absorbs, lining the kidney tubules and the small ducts that carry fluids to a surface.

labels.name: Simple columnar epithelium
labels.fn: One layer of tall cells with nuclei near the base, often with microvilli and goblet cells. It absorbs and secretes, lining the stomach and intestines.

labels.name: Stratified columnar epithelium
labels.fn: Several layers with tall cells at the surface. It is rare, found in parts of the male urethra and some large ducts.

labels.name: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium
labels.fn: One layer of cells of different heights, so the nuclei sit at different levels and it looks layered, though every cell touches the basement membrane. Ciliated with goblet cells, it lines the airways and sweeps mucus.

follow.q: Pseudostratified epithelium looks layered. Why is it still classed as a single layer?
options: Every cell rests on the basement membrane, though not all reach the surface
Its nuclei line up in a single row, even though the cells are stacked on top of each other
It has only one nucleus per row
follow.why: Layers are counted by contact with the basement membrane. In pseudostratified epithelium every cell rests on it; the cells differ in height, so their nuclei sit at different levels and fake the look of layers.

labels.name: Intercalated discs
labels.fn: The thick, dark lines where cardiac muscle fibers join end to end. Desmosomes in them hold the cells together as they pull, and gap junctions let electrical signals pass so the cells contract together.

follow.q: Which two junctions make up an intercalated disc?
follow.why: Heart cells must both hold together under strain and signal each other instantly. Desmosomes give the grip, and gap junctions let ions flow from cell to cell so the heart contracts as a unit.

labels.name: Capillary
labels.fn: The smallest blood vessel, with a wall one cell thick. Heart muscle is threaded with capillaries because it works nonstop and needs a steady oxygen supply.

labels.name: Desmosome
labels.fn: A spot weld in the intercalated disc that keeps neighboring heart muscle cells from pulling apart when they contract.

labels.name: Gap junction
labels.fn: Channels in the intercalated disc that let ions flow from one heart muscle cell to the next, so an electrical signal spreads and the cells contract together.

labels.name: Gap junction
labels.fn: Channels in the intercalated disc that let ions flow from one heart muscle cell to the next, so an electrical signal spreads and the cells contract together.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: The nucleus of a cardiac muscle fiber. Most cardiac fibers have one, near the center of the cell.

labels.name: Cardiac muscle fiber
labels.fn: A single heart muscle cell: striated, branched, usually with one central nucleus, and joined end to end to its neighbors at intercalated discs.

labels.name: Axon
labels.fn: The single long process that carries signals away from the neuron's cell body toward the next cell.

follow.q: Which way do signals travel along an axon?
options: Away from the cell body, toward the axon terminals
Toward the cell body from the axon terminals
follow.why: Dendrites and the cell body receive signals; the axon carries them away from the cell body to its terminals, where the neuron passes the signal on.

labels.name: Cell membrane
labels.fn: The plasma membrane of the neuron. Changes in the charge across it are the signals neurons carry.

labels.name: Dendrites
labels.fn: Short branching processes that receive signals from other neurons and carry them toward the cell body.

sets.title: Exocrine glands and modes of secretion

labels.name: Simple tubular
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with one unbranched duct and a straight tube of secretory cells, like the glands of the intestine.

labels.name: Simple alveolar (acinar)
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with one duct ending in a round sac (alveolus or acinus) of secretory cells. It occurs only as a stage in development.

labels.name: Surface epithelium
labels.fn: The epithelium covering the surface from which the gland grew down, and onto which its duct opens.

labels.name: Duct
labels.fn: The tube that carries an exocrine gland's product to a surface. Its presence is what makes a gland exocrine.

labels.name: Gland cells
labels.fn: The secretory cells of the gland, at the deep end of the duct. They make the product the duct carries away.

labels.name: Simple coiled tubular
labels.fn: An exocrine gland whose tube of secretory cells is coiled, like a sweat gland.

labels.name: Simple branched alveolar
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with one duct leading to several round secretory sacs, like the oil glands of the skin.

labels.name: Simple branched tubular
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with one duct leading to several branching tubes of secretory cells, like glands of the stomach.

labels.name: Compound alveolar (acinar)
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with a branched duct system leading to round secretory sacs, like the milk-making glands of the breast.

labels.name: Compound tubuloalveolar
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with a branched duct system and both tubes and sacs of secretory cells, like the larger glands that empty into the mouth and the exocrine pancreas.

labels.name: Compound tubular
labels.fn: An exocrine gland with a branched duct system leading to tube-shaped secretory parts, like the mucous glands of the mouth.

labels.name: Secretion
labels.fn: The product the gland cell releases.

labels.name: Secretory vesicle
labels.fn: A membrane bubble that buds from the Golgi apparatus carrying finished product. It fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell.

labels.name: Golgi complex
labels.fn: A stack of flattened membrane sacs that receives proteins and lipids from the ER, modifies and sorts them, and ships them out in vesicles to the membrane, to lysosomes or out of the cell.

follow.q: A protein made for export leaves the rough ER. Where does it go next?
options: To the Golgi apparatus, in a transport vesicle
Straight out of the cell through the membrane
follow.why: Proteins for export travel from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus in transport vesicles. The Golgi finishes and sorts them, then packs them into secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane.

labels.name: Merocrine secretion
labels.fn: Release of product by exocytosis: vesicles fuse with the membrane and empty outside, and the cell stays whole. The glands that make watery sweat secrete this way, and so do many glands that empty into the mouth.

follow.q: In which mode of secretion does the gland cell survive intact?
follow.why: In merocrine secretion only the contents of vesicles leave, by exocytosis, so the cell loses nothing of itself. In holocrine secretion the whole cell bursts, and classical apocrine secretion pinches off the top of the cell.

labels.name: Nucleus
labels.fn: The nucleus of the gland cell.

labels.name: Apocrine secretion
labels.fn: The classic description: product collects at the top of the cell, which pinches off with it. The milk-making glands of the breast release fat droplets this way. The glands in the armpit long called apocrine turn out to secrete mainly by exocytosis, so the name there is historical.

labels.name: Holocrine secretion
labels.fn: The whole cell fills with product, dies and breaks apart, becoming the secretion. New cells from below replace it. The oil (sebaceous) glands of the skin work this way.
