labels.fn: The branch of the left coronary artery that curves around the left side of the heart in the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle. It supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Right atrium
labels.fn: The upper right chamber. It receives blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae, plus the heart's own used blood, and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

follow.q: Which vessels empty into the right atrium?
options: The superior and inferior venae cavae
The left and right pulmonary arteries
follow.why: The venae cavae carry blood back from the body and open into the right atrium. The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and the pulmonary trunk and aorta leave the ventricles.

labels.name: Anterior interventricular artery
labels.fn: The branch of the left coronary artery that runs down the front of the heart between the two ventricles (also called the left anterior descending artery). It supplies the front of both ventricles and much of the interventricular septum.

follow.q: A clot blocks the anterior interventricular artery. Which region is most likely to be damaged?
options: The front of the left ventricle and the interventricular septum
The back of the right ventricle and the lower part of the right atrium
follow.why: This artery runs down the front groove between the ventricles and feeds the front wall of the left ventricle and most of the septum. Muscle downstream of a blocked artery loses its oxygen supply (ischemia) and can die (a myocardial infarction).

labels.name: Atrial arteries
labels.fn: Small branches of the coronary arteries that supply the walls of the atria.

labels.name: Anterior cardiac veins
labels.fn: Small veins on the front of the right ventricle that empty straight into the right atrium instead of into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Great cardiac vein
labels.fn: The vein that runs up the front of the heart beside the anterior interventricular artery, collecting deoxygenated blood from the front of the ventricles and carrying it into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Small cardiac vein
labels.fn: A vein along the lower right edge of the heart that drains the right side and empties into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Marginal artery
labels.fn: A branch of the right coronary artery that runs along the lower right edge of the heart and supplies the right ventricle.

labels.name: Coronary sinus
labels.fn: A wide vein in the groove on the back of the heart between the atria and ventricles. It gathers blood from most of the cardiac veins and empties it into the right atrium.

follow.q: Where does the coronary sinus empty?
follow.why: The heart's own used, deoxygenated blood collects in the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium beside the inferior vena cava. From there it joins the rest of the body's returning blood.

labels.name: Small cardiac vein
labels.fn: A vein along the lower right edge of the heart that drains the right side and empties into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Circumflex artery
labels.fn: The branch of the left coronary artery that curves around the left side of the heart in the groove between the left atrium and left ventricle. It supplies the left atrium and the side and back of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Great cardiac vein
labels.fn: The vein that runs up the front of the heart beside the anterior interventricular artery, collecting deoxygenated blood from the front of the ventricles and carrying it into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Marginal artery
labels.fn: A marginal branch of the circumflex artery that runs down the left edge of the heart and supplies the side wall of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Posterior interventricular artery
labels.fn: The artery that runs down the back of the heart between the ventricles, usually from the right coronary artery. It supplies the back of both ventricles and it meets branches of the anterior interventricular artery near the apex (an anastomosis).

labels.name: Posterior cardiac vein
labels.fn: A vein on the back of the left ventricle that drains it into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Left ventricle
labels.fn: The lower left chamber and the heart's main pump. It pushes blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to the whole body, which takes high pressure, so its wall is the thickest in the heart.

follow.q: For years, the pressure in a person's body arteries has been well above normal. Which chamber's wall thickens most?
follow.why: The left ventricle must raise its pressure above the pressure in the aorta before its valve opens. Higher arterial pressure means more work every beat, and muscle that works harder grows thicker.

labels.name: Right coronary artery
labels.fn: The first branch of the aorta on the right, running in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle. It supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle and, in most people, the back of the heart.

follow.q: Where do the coronary arteries branch from?
options: The base of the aorta, just past the aortic valve
The pulmonary trunk, just past the pulmonary valve
follow.why: The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, leaving it just beyond the aortic valve. They fill mainly when the ventricles relax (diastole), when the heart muscle is not squeezing them shut.

labels.name: Middle cardiac vein
labels.fn: The vein on the back of the heart beside the posterior interventricular artery. It drains the back of the ventricles into the coronary sinus.

labels.name: Marginal artery
labels.fn: A branch of the right coronary artery that runs along the lower right edge of the heart and supplies the right ventricle.

labels.name: Arch of aorta
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart, turning up, back and to the left over the pulmonary trunk. Beyond it, the aorta runs down behind the heart.

labels.name: Bachmann’s bundle
labels.fn: A band of conducting fibers that carries the SA node's signal across to the left atrium, so both atria contract almost together.

labels.name: Sinoatrial (SA) node
labels.fn: A cluster of autorhythmic cells in the wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava. It depolarizes on its own fastest, so it sets the heart rate: the heart's pacemaker.

follow.q: Why does the SA node, and not the AV node, normally set the heart rate?
options: Its cells reach threshold on their own faster than any other autorhythmic cells
It is the only part of the heart whose cells can depolarize on their own without a signal
It receives the most blood from the coronary arteries
It is the largest mass of conducting tissue
follow.why: Several parts of the conduction system can fire on their own, but the SA node's pacemaker potential rises fastest. Its action potential sweeps through the heart and resets the slower cells before they reach threshold themselves.

labels.name: Left atrium
labels.fn: The upper left chamber. It receives blood returning from the lungs through the four pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve to the left ventricle.

follow.q: Blood entering the left atrium has just come from where?
options: The lungs, through the pulmonary veins
The body, through the venae cavae
The right atrium, through the interatrial septum
The left ventricle, through the mitral valve
follow.why: The pulmonary veins drain the lungs into the left atrium. After birth the interatrial septum is closed, and the mitral valve lets blood move only from atrium to ventricle, never back.

labels.name: Anterior internodal
labels.fn: One of three preferred routes through the right atrial muscle that carry the signal from the SA node toward the AV node a little faster. They are not insulated cables like the bundle branches.

labels.name: Atrioventricular (AV) node
labels.fn: A cluster of conducting cells in the floor of the right atrium near the septum. It conducts slowly, delaying the signal about a tenth of a second so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract. It is the only normal path from atria to ventricles.

follow.q: What does the delay at the AV node accomplish?
options: It gives the atria time to finish filling the ventricles before they contract
It lets the SA node's cells recover and repolarize before they fire the next beat
It lets the coronary arteries fill
It keeps the two atria from contracting together
follow.why: The cardiac skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles everywhere except where the AV bundle passes through it, and conduction through the AV node just above it is slow. That pause lets atrial contraction top up the ventricles; if the ventricles fired at the same moment, the atria would be squeezing against closed valves.

labels.name: Atrioventricular (AV) bundle (bundle of His)
labels.fn: The bundle of His: the only conducting link through the insulating cardiac skeleton, carrying the signal from the AV node into the top of the interventricular septum.

labels.name: Middle internodal
labels.fn: One of three preferred routes through the right atrial muscle that carry the signal from the SA node toward the AV node a little faster. They are not insulated cables like the bundle branches.

labels.name: Posterior internodal
labels.fn: One of three preferred routes through the right atrial muscle that carry the signal from the SA node toward the AV node a little faster. They are not insulated cables like the bundle branches.

labels.name: Left ventricle
labels.fn: The lower left chamber and the heart's main pump. It pushes blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to the whole body, which takes high pressure, so its wall is the thickest in the heart.

follow.q: For years, the pressure in a person's body arteries has been well above normal. Which chamber's wall thickens most?
follow.why: The left ventricle must raise its pressure above the pressure in the aorta before its valve opens. Higher arterial pressure means more work every beat, and muscle that works harder grows thicker.

labels.name: Right atrium
labels.fn: The upper right chamber. It receives blood returning from the body through the superior and inferior venae cavae, plus the heart's own used blood, and passes it through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle.

follow.q: Which vessels empty into the right atrium?
options: The superior and inferior venae cavae
The left and right pulmonary arteries
follow.why: The venae cavae carry blood back from the body and open into the right atrium. The pulmonary veins return blood from the lungs to the left atrium, and the pulmonary trunk and aorta leave the ventricles.

labels.name: Right ventricle
labels.fn: The lower right chamber. It pumps blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk and on to the lungs. The lungs are close and offer little resistance, so its wall is much thinner than the left ventricle's.

follow.q: Why is the right ventricle's wall thinner than the left ventricle's?
options: It pumps only to the nearby lungs, which need far lower pressure than the whole body
It pumps less blood per beat than the left ventricle
It receives blood with less oxygen, so its own muscle is weaker and cannot grow as thick
Its wall is thinned by the pressure of the lungs pressing on it
follow.why: Both ventricles pump the same volume per beat. The difference is pressure: pushing blood through the short, low-resistance route to the lungs takes far less pressure than pushing it through the whole body, so the right ventricle builds less muscle.

labels.name: Right and left bundle branches
labels.fn: The two branches of the AV bundle that run down either side of the interventricular septum toward the apex, carrying the signal to each ventricle.

labels.name: Purkinje fibers
labels.fn: Large, fast-conducting fibers that spread from the bundle branches through the ventricle walls, starting at the apex. They make the ventricles contract from the apex upward, squeezing blood toward the exits.

follow.q: Purkinje fibers deliver the signal to the apex first. Why does that matter?
options: The ventricles contract from the apex up, pushing blood toward the valves at the top
It lets the atria finish contracting before the ventricles start to squeeze from the top down
It keeps the AV valves open during contraction
follow.why: The exits from the ventricles are at the top. Contraction that starts at the apex and moves upward squeezes blood toward them, like squeezing a tube of toothpaste from the closed end.

sets.title: Vessel walls: arteries, capillaries and veins

labels.name: Elastic artery
labels.fn: The largest arteries, next to the heart, such as the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Their tunica media holds many sheets of elastic fibers that stretch with each ejection and recoil between beats, so pressure and flow do not drop to zero in diastole.

follow.q: Why does pressure in the aorta stay near 80 mm Hg between heartbeats instead of falling to zero?
options: Elastic fibers stretched during ejection recoil and keep pushing blood onward
The smooth muscle of the aorta contracts in rhythm with the heart
The aortic valve leaks a little blood back into the aorta
Veins push blood back into the aorta
follow.why: During ejection the elastic wall stretches and stores some of the energy of the beat. When the aortic valve closes the fibers recoil, squeezing blood onward during diastole. A stiffer aorta, as with age, recoils less and pressure falls lower between beats.

labels.name: Tunica externa
labels.fn: The outer coat of the elastic artery: connective tissue, mostly collagen, that anchors the vessel to nearby tissue and limits stretching. In the largest vessels it carries the vasa vasorum that feed the outer wall.

labels.name: Tunica media
labels.fn: The middle coat of the elastic artery. Smooth muscle cells lie between many layers of elastic fibers, so this wall acts mainly as a rubbery pressure reservoir.

labels.name: Tunica intima
labels.fn: The lining of the elastic artery: endothelium (simple squamous epithelium) on a basement membrane, with a thin layer of connective tissue and an internal elastic membrane. It gives blood a smooth surface.

labels.name: Muscular artery
labels.fn: A medium-sized, named artery that carries blood to one organ or region. Its thick tunica media is mostly smooth muscle, so nerves can narrow or widen it and shift blood between regions.

follow.q: What does the thick smooth muscle of a muscular artery allow that an elastic artery cannot do as well?
options: Change its diameter to adjust how much blood reaches a region
Store energy from each heartbeat and release it in diastole
Exchange gases with the tissue around it
Hold blood in reserve at low pressure
follow.why: Muscular arteries have fewer elastic fibers and many layers of smooth muscle. When sympathetic nerves change how contracted that muscle is, the vessel narrows or widens and the share of blood going to that region changes.

labels.name: Tunica externa
labels.fn: The outer collagen coat of the muscular artery. It is relatively thick here and anchors the artery to the tissues it runs through.

labels.name: Tunica media
labels.fn: The middle coat of the muscular artery, and its thickest layer: many rings of smooth muscle with few elastic fibers. Its contraction narrows the vessel (vasoconstriction); its relaxation widens it (vasodilation).

labels.name: Tunica intima
labels.fn: The lining of the muscular artery: endothelium on a basement membrane, edged by a wavy internal elastic membrane. Endothelial cells release signals that act on the smooth muscle beneath them.

labels.name: Arteriole
labels.fn: The smallest artery, under about 0.1 mm across, with one to a few layers of smooth muscle. Because resistance depends so steeply on radius, arterioles are the main resistance vessels and decide how much blood each capillary bed receives.

follow.q: Halving an arteriole's radius raises its resistance to flow about how much?
follow.why: Resistance varies with 1 divided by the radius to the fourth power. Half the radius gives 2 to the fourth, or 16 times the resistance. That is why small changes in arteriolar tone make large changes in flow and pressure.

labels.name: Tunica externa
labels.fn: The thin outer connective tissue coat of the arteriole. In the smallest arterioles it is only a few scattered fibers.

labels.name: Tunica media
labels.fn: The arteriole's one to a few layers of smooth muscle. Kept partly contracted all the time (vascular tone), it can narrow or widen the arteriole and so control flow into the capillaries beyond.

labels.name: Tunica intima
labels.fn: The endothelial lining of the arteriole, on its basement membrane. It is the only layer that continues on into the capillaries.

labels.name: Continuous
labels.fn: The most common capillary type: an unbroken sheet of endothelial cells on a complete basement membrane. Water and small solutes pass through the narrow clefts between cells; proteins and blood cells stay inside. Found in skin, muscle and connective tissue.

follow.q: A continuous capillary lets glucose through but keeps plasma proteins in the blood. What explains that?
options: The only route across is narrow clefts between endothelial cells, too small for proteins
Its endothelial cells have pores sized so that glucose fits through but proteins are too big
Smooth muscle in its wall squeezes proteins back
follow.why: In a continuous capillary the endothelial cells form an unbroken sheet on a complete basement membrane. Small solutes such as glucose and ions slip through the thin clefts between cells, but large proteins are too big, so they stay in the plasma.

labels.name: Fenestrated
labels.fn: A capillary with small pores through the endothelial cells themselves, on an intact basement membrane. The pores let fluid and small molecules cross much faster, where tissues filter or absorb a lot of fluid, such as the lining of the intestine and hormone-releasing glands.

labels.name: Sinusoid
labels.fn: A wide, twisting capillary with large gaps between endothelial cells and an incomplete basement membrane. Proteins and even whole blood cells can pass, as in the liver, spleen and red bone marrow.

follow.q: Why would red bone marrow need sinusoid capillaries rather than continuous ones?
options: New blood cells must be able to pass through the wall into the blood
Bone marrow needs a higher blood pressure
Sinusoids keep plasma proteins out of the marrow so they do not clog the new cells
Sinusoids have more smooth muscle to control flow
follow.why: Sinusoids have large gaps between endothelial cells and an incomplete basement membrane, so whole cells can cross. New blood cells made in the marrow enter the circulation that way; a continuous capillary would hold them back.

labels.name: Basement membrane
labels.fn: The thin sheet of protein fibers under the endothelium, made partly by the endothelial cells. In continuous and fenestrated capillaries it is complete and acts as an extra filter.

labels.name: Endothelial layer (tunica intima)
labels.fn: The capillary wall itself: a single layer of flat endothelial cells, the same simple squamous lining as the tunica intima of larger vessels. With no muscle or outer coat, the diffusion distance between blood and tissue is tiny.

labels.name: Incomplete basement membrane
labels.fn: The broken, patchy basement membrane of a sinusoid. Together with the wide gaps between its cells, it lets proteins and cells cross the wall.

labels.name: Intercellular gap
labels.fn: A wide opening between neighboring endothelial cells in a sinusoid, large enough for proteins and blood cells to pass.

labels.name: Intercellular cleft
labels.fn: A narrow slit between neighboring endothelial cells in a continuous capillary. Water, ions and small solutes such as glucose move through it; large proteins do not.

labels.name: Large vein
labels.fn: A large vein near the heart, such as a vena cava. Pressure inside is low, so its tunica media is thin; its thickest layer is the collagen-rich tunica externa, which also holds bundles of smooth muscle running along its length.

follow.q: Compared with an artery of similar size, a vein has a thinner tunica media and a wider lumen. Why does that suit it?
options: Its blood is at low pressure, and a thin, wide vessel can hold a large volume
Veins must withstand higher pressure than arteries, and a wide lumen spreads that pressure out
Veins exchange gases through their walls
A thin wall keeps blood from flowing backward
follow.why: Most of the pressure from the heart is used up in the arterioles and capillaries, so veins carry blood at low pressure. A thin, compliant wall with a wide lumen lets them hold much of the blood volume; valves, not wall thickness, stop backflow.

labels.name: Tunica externa
labels.fn: The outer coat of the large vein, and its thickest layer: collagen-rich connective tissue with longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle, the vasa vasorum and the nervi vasorum.

labels.name: Tunica media
labels.fn: The middle coat of the large vein: only a thin layer of smooth muscle with few elastic fibers, because the pressure it faces is low.

labels.name: Tunica intima
labels.fn: The endothelial lining of the large vein on its basement membrane, giving blood a smooth surface to flow over.

labels.name: Smooth muscle cell in tunica externa
labels.fn: Smooth muscle cells running lengthwise in the tunica externa of a large vein. They are a feature of the largest veins; in arteries the smooth muscle sits in the tunica media instead.

labels.name: Vasa vasorum
labels.fn: Tiny blood vessels in the outer wall of a large vessel, the "vessels of the vessels." Nutrients from the lumen diffuse only a short way, so these supply the outer layers of a thick wall.

follow.q: Why do large vessels need vasa vasorum, while capillaries do not?
options: Diffusion from the lumen reaches only a short way into a thick wall
Blood inside large vessels has too little oxygen left to supply the cells of their walls
Vasa vasorum carry the nerve signals to the wall
Vasa vasorum drain excess fluid from the lumen
follow.why: A capillary wall is one cell thick, so every cell is right next to the blood. The outer layers of a large artery or vein are too far from the lumen for diffusion to feed them, so small vessels in the tunica externa supply them.

labels.name: Nervi vasorum
labels.fn: Nerves in the vessel wall, the "nerves of the vessels." They are sympathetic fibers that reach the smooth muscle and control how contracted it is.

labels.name: Medium-sized vein
labels.fn: A vein of the limbs and organs. It has a thin tunica media, a thicker tunica externa and, especially in the limbs, valves that keep blood moving toward the heart.

labels.name: Tunica externa
labels.fn: The outer collagen coat of the medium-sized vein, its thickest layer, which anchors it to surrounding tissue.

labels.name: Tunica media
labels.fn: The thin middle coat of the medium-sized vein: a few layers of smooth muscle with little elastic tissue.

labels.name: Tunica intima
labels.fn: The endothelial lining of the medium-sized vein. Its folds form the venous valves.

labels.name: Valves (closed)
labels.fn: Venous valves: paired flaps formed from folds of the tunica intima. Blood flowing toward the heart pushes them open; blood starting to fall back fills their pockets and snaps them shut.

follow.q: Venous valves in the legs fail and blood pools in superficial veins. Which change follows?
options: The veins stretch and bulge because blood falls back and collects in them
Arterial pressure in the legs falls to zero
Blood flows faster back to the heart
The capillaries of the legs stop filling, and the skin of the legs turns pale and cold
follow.why: Valves hold up the column of blood between the muscle squeezes that push it upward. When they fail, blood falls back and pools; the thin-walled veins stretch and twist into varicose veins.

labels.name: Venule
labels.fn: The smallest vein, draining a capillary bed. The first venules are little more than endothelium; larger ones gain a thin coat of smooth muscle. Their walls are leaky enough for white blood cells to squeeze out into tissue.

labels.name: Tunica externa
labels.fn: The thin outer connective tissue coat of the venule.

labels.name: Tunica media
labels.fn: The venule's middle coat: at most a thin layer of smooth muscle, absent in the smallest venules.

labels.name: Tunica intima
labels.fn: The endothelial lining of the venule, continuous with the endothelium of the capillaries that drain into it.

labels.name: Vertebral
labels.fn: A branch of each subclavian artery that climbs through the neck bones to the base of the brain, where the two join to form the basilar artery.

labels.name: Right common carotid
labels.fn: The artery up the right side of the neck, from the brachiocephalic trunk. At the level of the upper neck it splits into the internal carotid (brain) and external carotid (face and scalp) arteries.

labels.name: Right subclavian
labels.fn: The artery to the right arm, from the brachiocephalic trunk. It passes under the collarbone and becomes the axillary artery in the armpit; it also gives off the right vertebral artery.

labels.name: Left common carotid
labels.fn: The artery up the left side of the neck, branching straight from the aortic arch. It splits into the internal carotid artery to the brain and the external carotid artery to the face and scalp.

follow.q: Where would you press to feel the carotid pulse?
options: At the side of the neck, beside the windpipe
On the inner wrist below the thumb
follow.why: The common carotid arteries run up either side of the neck next to the trachea, close to the skin, so each heartbeat's pressure wave can be felt there. The wrist, groin and knee sites are the radial, femoral and popliteal pulses.

labels.name: Left subclavian
labels.fn: The artery to the left arm, the last branch of the aortic arch. It passes under the collarbone, gives off the left vertebral artery and becomes the axillary artery.

labels.name: Brachiocephalic trunk
labels.fn: The first branch of the aortic arch, on the right. It is short and splits into the right common carotid artery (to the head) and the right subclavian artery (to the right arm). There is no left brachiocephalic trunk.

labels.name: Axillary
labels.fn: The continuation of the subclavian artery through the armpit (the axilla). At the arm it becomes the brachial artery.

labels.name: Aortic arch
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart, turning back and to the left. Its three branches supply the head and arms: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery.

follow.q: Which vessel is NOT a branch of the aortic arch?
follow.why: On the right side the arch gives one trunk, the brachiocephalic trunk, which then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian leave the arch directly, so of the two common carotid arteries only the left one branches straight from the arch.

labels.name: Pulmonary trunk
labels.fn: The short, wide vessel that leaves the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries. It carries blood to the lungs.

follow.q: Which chamber pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk?
follow.why: The pulmonary valve sits between the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk. The left ventricle pumps into the aorta, and the atria pump only into the ventricles.

labels.name: Ascending aorta
labels.fn: The first part of the aorta, rising from the left ventricle. Its only branches are the right and left coronary arteries.

labels.name: Descending aorta
labels.fn: The long part of the aorta that runs down behind the heart and through the diaphragm. Above the diaphragm it is the thoracic aorta; below it, the abdominal aorta.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped muscle between the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. The descending aorta passes behind it through an opening called the aortic hiatus; above that point it is the thoracic aorta, below it the abdominal aorta.

labels.name: Celiac trunk
labels.fn: The first unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta, just below the diaphragm. It quickly splits to supply the stomach, liver, spleen and part of the pancreas.

labels.name: Renal
labels.fn: A paired branch of the abdominal aorta to each kidney. The kidneys receive about a fifth of the heart's output at rest, so these are short, wide arteries.

labels.name: Brachial
labels.fn: The main artery of the upper arm, continuing from the axillary artery. It runs along the inner arm and is where blood pressure is measured with a cuff; at the elbow it splits into the radial and ulnar arteries.

follow.q: Blood pressure cuffs are placed on the upper arm because they compress which artery?
follow.why: The brachial artery runs close to the skin along the inner upper arm, at about the level of the heart, so a cuff can squeeze it shut and a stethoscope at the elbow can hear flow return.

labels.name: Superior mesenteric
labels.fn: An unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta just below the celiac trunk. It supplies most of the gut below the stomach: the long, narrow part where most food is absorbed and the first half of the wider part that follows.

labels.name: Gonadal
labels.fn: A paired, slender branch of the abdominal aorta to the testes or ovaries (the testicular or ovarian artery).

labels.name: Inferior mesenteric
labels.fn: The lowest unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta. It supplies the last part of the gut, down to the upper part of its last straight stretch. Branches of the internal iliac artery supply the lowest few centimeters.

labels.name: Radial
labels.fn: The forearm artery on the thumb side, from the brachial artery. At the wrist it lies just under the skin over the bone, where the radial pulse is taken.

labels.name: Common iliac
labels.fn: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta. Each splits into an internal iliac artery to the pelvis and an external iliac artery to the leg.

labels.name: Ulnar
labels.fn: The forearm artery on the little-finger side, from the brachial artery. It joins the radial artery in the palm through the palmar arches.

labels.name: Internal iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery that supplies the pelvic organs, the buttocks and the inner thigh.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery headed to the leg. It passes under the ligament in the groin and becomes the femoral artery.

labels.name: Palmar arches
labels.fn: Arching connections between the radial and ulnar arteries in the palm. Because blood can reach the fingers from either artery, the hand keeps its supply if one of them is blocked.

labels.name: Deep femoral
labels.fn: The large branch of the femoral artery that runs deep in the thigh and supplies the thigh muscles and the femur.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The main artery of the thigh, continuing from the external iliac artery. In the groin it lies close to the skin, where the femoral pulse is felt and where catheters are often inserted.

labels.name: Descending genicular
labels.fn: A small branch of the femoral artery that runs down to the inner side of the knee and helps supply the knee joint.

labels.name: Popliteal
labels.fn: The continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee, where the popliteal pulse is felt. Below the knee it splits into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.

labels.name: Posterior tibial
labels.fn: The branch of the popliteal artery down the back of the leg. It passes behind the bump on the inner ankle, where its pulse is felt, and continues into the sole of the foot.

labels.name: Anterior tibial
labels.fn: The branch of the popliteal artery to the front of the leg. At the ankle it becomes the dorsalis pedis artery on top of the foot.

labels.name: Fibular
labels.fn: A branch of the posterior tibial artery that runs down the outer side of the leg and supplies the muscles there (also called the peroneal artery).

labels.name: Dorsalis pedis
labels.fn: The continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the top of the foot, where the pedal pulse is felt. Checking it tells you blood is reaching the end of the leg.

labels.name: Plantar arch
labels.fn: The arching artery in the sole of the foot, fed by the posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries. It supplies the toes from two directions.

labels.name: Right common carotid artery
labels.fn: The artery up the right side of the neck, from the brachiocephalic trunk. At the level of the upper neck it splits into the internal carotid (brain) and external carotid (face and scalp) arteries.

labels.name: Left common carotid artery
labels.fn: The artery up the left side of the neck, branching straight from the aortic arch. It splits into the internal carotid artery to the brain and the external carotid artery to the face and scalp.

follow.q: Where would you press to feel the carotid pulse?
options: At the side of the neck, beside the windpipe
On the inner wrist below the thumb
follow.why: The common carotid arteries run up either side of the neck next to the trachea, close to the skin, so each heartbeat's pressure wave can be felt there. The wrist, groin and knee sites are the radial, femoral and popliteal pulses.

labels.name: Right subclavian artery
labels.fn: The artery to the right arm, from the brachiocephalic trunk. It passes under the collarbone and becomes the axillary artery in the armpit; it also gives off the right vertebral artery.

labels.name: Left subclavian artery
labels.fn: The artery to the left arm, the last branch of the aortic arch. It passes under the collarbone, gives off the left vertebral artery and becomes the axillary artery.

labels.name: Brachiocephalic artery
labels.fn: The first branch of the aortic arch, on the right. It is short and splits into the right common carotid artery (to the head) and the right subclavian artery (to the right arm). There is no left brachiocephalic trunk.

labels.name: Aortic arch
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart, turning back and to the left. Its three branches supply the head and arms: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery.

follow.q: Which vessel is NOT a branch of the aortic arch?
follow.why: On the right side the arch gives one trunk, the brachiocephalic trunk, which then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian leave the arch directly, so of the two common carotid arteries only the left one branches straight from the arch.

labels.name: Ascending aorta
labels.fn: The first part of the aorta, rising from the left ventricle. Its only branches are the right and left coronary arteries.

labels.name: Descending aorta
labels.fn: The long part of the aorta that runs down behind the heart and through the diaphragm. Above the diaphragm it is the thoracic aorta; below it, the abdominal aorta.

labels.name: Left coronary artery
labels.fn: The first branch of the aorta on the left. After a short course it splits into the anterior interventricular artery and the circumflex artery, which together supply most of the left ventricle.

labels.name: Right coronary artery
labels.fn: The first branch of the aorta on the right, running in the groove between the right atrium and right ventricle. It supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle and, in most people, the back of the heart.

follow.q: Where do the coronary arteries branch from?
options: The base of the aorta, just past the aortic valve
The pulmonary trunk, just past the pulmonary valve
follow.why: The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, leaving it just beyond the aortic valve. They fill mainly when the ventricles relax (diastole), when the heart muscle is not squeezing them shut.

labels.name: Thoracic aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta above the diaphragm. It gives small branches to the chest wall, esophagus and airways before passing through the aortic hiatus.

labels.name: Abdominal aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta below the diaphragm. It gives off the celiac trunk, the mesenteric, renal and gonadal arteries, and ends by splitting into the two common iliac arteries.

follow.q: The abdominal aorta ends by dividing into which pair of arteries?
follow.why: At about the level of the navel the abdominal aorta splits into the right and left common iliac arteries. Each then divides into an internal iliac (pelvis) and an external iliac, which becomes the femoral artery in the thigh.

labels.name: Anterior communicating
labels.fn: A short link between the two anterior cerebral arteries at the front of the cerebral arterial circle. It lets blood cross from one side to the other.

labels.name: Middle cerebral
labels.fn: The largest branch of the internal carotid artery. It runs out to the side of the brain and supplies most of its outer surface, so it is the artery most often blocked when a clot cuts off blood flow to part of the brain.

labels.name: Anterior cerebral
labels.fn: A branch of the internal carotid artery that runs forward and up between the two halves of the brain, supplying their inner surfaces.

labels.name: Ophthalmic
labels.fn: A branch of the internal carotid artery that supplies the eye and the structures around it.

labels.name: Posterior communicating
labels.fn: A short link on each side of the cerebral arterial circle between the internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries. It connects the front and back blood supplies of the brain.

follow.q: Why does a slowly narrowing internal carotid artery often cause no symptoms at first?
options: Blood reaches that side around the cerebral arterial circle
The brain can store enough oxygen for weeks
The external carotid artery takes over supplying the brain directly
The vertebral arteries grow larger within days
follow.why: The communicating arteries join the carotid and basilar supplies into a ring. If one input narrows slowly, blood can flow around the ring from the others. This is an anastomosis; it cannot help if the blockage is sudden and downstream of the circle.

labels.name: Posterior cerebral
labels.fn: A branch of the basilar artery that supplies the back of the brain, including the area for vision.

labels.name: Internal carotid
labels.fn: The branch of the common carotid artery that enters the skull and supplies most of the front of the brain and the eye. It joins the cerebral arterial circle at the base of the brain.

labels.name: Basilar
labels.fn: The single artery formed where the two vertebral arteries join on the underside of the brainstem. It supplies the brainstem and the back of the brain and feeds the cerebral arterial circle.

labels.name: Vertebral
labels.fn: A branch of each subclavian artery that climbs through the neck bones to the base of the brain, where the two join to form the basilar artery.

labels.name: Aortic arch
labels.fn: The curve of the aorta above the heart, turning back and to the left. Its three branches supply the head and arms: the brachiocephalic trunk, the left common carotid artery and the left subclavian artery.

follow.q: Which vessel is NOT a branch of the aortic arch?
follow.why: On the right side the arch gives one trunk, the brachiocephalic trunk, which then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian leave the arch directly, so of the two common carotid arteries only the left one branches straight from the arch.

labels.name: Internal thoracic
labels.fn: A branch of the subclavian artery that runs down the inside of the front chest wall beside the sternum, supplying the chest wall. Surgeons often use it to bypass a blocked coronary artery.

labels.name: Esophageal
labels.fn: Small branches of the thoracic aorta that supply the esophagus.

labels.name: Intercostal
labels.fn: Paired arteries that run along the lower edge of each rib, supplying the intercostal muscles and the chest wall. Most branch from the thoracic aorta.

labels.name: Mediastinal
labels.fn: Small branches of the thoracic aorta that supply the tissues of the mediastinum.

labels.name: Pericardial
labels.fn: Small branches of the thoracic aorta that supply the back of the pericardium.

labels.name: Superior phrenic
labels.fn: Small branches of the thoracic aorta that supply the upper surface of the diaphragm (phren- means diaphragm).

labels.name: Thoracic aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta above the diaphragm. It gives small branches to the chest wall, esophagus and airways before passing through the aortic hiatus.

labels.name: Aortic hiatus
labels.fn: The opening at the back of the diaphragm through which the descending aorta passes. Above it the vessel is the thoracic aorta, below it the abdominal aorta.

labels.name: Inferior phrenic
labels.fn: The first branches of the abdominal aorta, supplying the underside of the diaphragm.

labels.name: Celiac trunk
labels.fn: The first unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta, just below the diaphragm. It quickly splits to supply the stomach, liver, spleen and part of the pancreas.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominopelvic cavity. The heart rests on its upper surface, tilted so the apex points down and to your left.

labels.name: Left gastric
labels.fn: A branch of the celiac trunk that supplies the lesser curve of the stomach and the lower esophagus.

labels.name: Adrenal
labels.fn: Small paired branches of the abdominal aorta (the middle suprarenal arteries) that supply the adrenal glands on top of the kidneys.

labels.name: Splenic
labels.fn: The largest branch of the celiac trunk. It runs to the left behind the stomach to the spleen, giving branches to the stomach and pancreas on the way.

labels.name: Common hepatic
labels.fn: A branch of the celiac trunk that runs to the right. It gives off branches to the stomach and continues as the hepatic artery proper, which brings oxygenated blood to the liver.

labels.name: Renal
labels.fn: A paired branch of the abdominal aorta to each kidney. The kidneys receive about a fifth of the heart's output at rest, so these are short, wide arteries.

labels.name: Gonadal
labels.fn: A paired, slender branch of the abdominal aorta to the testes or ovaries (the testicular or ovarian artery).

labels.name: Superior mesenteric
labels.fn: An unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta just below the celiac trunk. It supplies most of the gut below the stomach: the long, narrow part where most food is absorbed and the first half of the wider part that follows.

labels.name: Lumbar
labels.fn: Paired branches from the back of the abdominal aorta that supply the lower back muscles, the lumbar vertebrae and the spinal cord.

labels.name: Abdominal aorta
labels.fn: The descending aorta below the diaphragm. It gives off the celiac trunk, the mesenteric, renal and gonadal arteries, and ends by splitting into the two common iliac arteries.

follow.q: The abdominal aorta ends by dividing into which pair of arteries?
follow.why: At about the level of the navel the abdominal aorta splits into the right and left common iliac arteries. Each then divides into an internal iliac (pelvis) and an external iliac, which becomes the femoral artery in the thigh.

labels.name: Median sacral
labels.fn: A small, single artery that continues from the back of the aorta where it splits, running down the front of the sacrum and coccyx.

labels.name: Inferior mesenteric
labels.fn: The lowest unpaired branch of the abdominal aorta. It supplies the last part of the gut, down to the upper part of its last straight stretch. Branches of the internal iliac artery supply the lowest few centimeters.

labels.name: Common iliac
labels.fn: One of the two terminal branches of the abdominal aorta. Each splits into an internal iliac artery to the pelvis and an external iliac artery to the leg.

labels.name: Internal iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery that supplies the pelvic organs, the buttocks and the inner thigh.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The branch of the common iliac artery headed to the leg. It passes under the ligament in the groin and becomes the femoral artery.

labels.name: Temporal artery
labels.fn: The superficial temporal artery, a branch of the external carotid artery that runs up in front of the ear. Its pulse can be felt just in front of the ear.

labels.name: Facial artery
labels.fn: A branch of the external carotid artery that crosses the lower edge of the jaw on its way to the face. Its pulse can be felt where it crosses the jaw.

labels.name: Common carotid artery
labels.fn: The large artery up each side of the neck. Its pulse, felt beside the trachea, is the one to check in an unresponsive person, because it is strong and close to the heart.

follow.q: Why is the carotid pulse often still felt when the radial pulse is not?
options: The carotid is large and near the heart, so a weak pressure wave still reaches it
The carotid artery has a band of heart muscle in its wall that pumps with every beat
The radial artery is a vein
The carotid pulse is caused by breathing
follow.why: Each beat sends a pressure wave outward from the heart. When pressure is low, the wave is still strong enough to feel in a large artery close to the heart but fades before it reaches a small artery at the wrist.

labels.name: Brachial artery
labels.fn: The main artery of the upper arm. Its pulse is felt on the inner side of the elbow, and it is the artery heard with a stethoscope when blood pressure is taken.

labels.name: Radial artery
labels.fn: The forearm artery on the thumb side. Its pulse is felt on the inner wrist just below the thumb, the most common place to count a heart rate.

labels.name: Femoral artery
labels.fn: The main artery of the thigh. Its pulse is felt in the groin, midway between the bony point of the hip and the pubic bone.

labels.name: Popliteal artery
labels.fn: The artery behind the knee. Its pulse is felt deep in the back of the knee, easiest with the knee slightly bent.

labels.name: Posterior tibial artery
labels.fn: The artery that passes behind the bump on the inner ankle, where its pulse is felt.

labels.name: Dorsalis pedis artery
labels.fn: The artery on the top of the foot. Its pulse (the pedal pulse) shows whether blood is reaching the end of the leg.

labels.name: External jugular
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the side of the neck that drains the scalp and face. It is often visible when a person strains or lies flat, and it empties into the subclavian vein.

labels.name: Internal jugular
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the neck, beside the common carotid artery. It drains the brain (from the dural venous sinuses), face and neck and joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

labels.name: Subclavian
labels.fn: The continuation of the axillary vein under the collarbone. It drains the arm and joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. It is a common site for a central line.

labels.name: Brachiocephalic
labels.fn: Each side has one: formed where the internal jugular and subclavian veins meet, behind the collarbone. The right and left brachiocephalic veins join to form the superior vena cava. Unlike the artery, there are two.

follow.q: How does venous drainage of the head differ from its arterial supply at the root of the neck?
options: There are two brachiocephalic veins but only one brachiocephalic artery (trunk)
There are two brachiocephalic arteries but no brachiocephalic veins
Veins from the head drain straight into the right atrium
The jugular veins join the aorta
follow.why: On the arterial side only the right has a brachiocephalic trunk; the left carotid and subclavian leave the aortic arch directly. On the venous side both sides form a brachiocephalic vein, and the two merge into the superior vena cava.

labels.name: Axillary
labels.fn: The large vein of the armpit, formed by the basilic and brachial veins and joined by the cephalic vein. It becomes the subclavian vein.

labels.name: Cephalic
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the thumb side of the arm. It runs up to the shoulder and empties into the axillary vein, and is often used for IV lines.

labels.name: Superior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and chest to the right atrium, entering it from above.

follow.q: Blood from your right arm reaches the heart through which vessel?
follow.why: Veins above the diaphragm, including those of the arms, head and neck, drain into the superior vena cava, which opens into the right atrium. The inferior vena cava drains the body below the diaphragm.

labels.name: Brachial
labels.fn: The paired deep veins that run beside the brachial artery in the upper arm and join the basilic vein to form the axillary vein.

labels.name: Intercostal
labels.fn: Veins along the lower edge of each rib that drain the chest wall, mostly into the azygos system.

labels.name: Basilic
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the little-finger side of the arm. It dives deep partway up the arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.

labels.name: Hepatic
labels.fn: The veins that carry blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava, just below the diaphragm. This blood has already passed through both the gut's capillaries and the liver's.

labels.name: Inferior vena cava
labels.fn: The largest vein in the body. It returns blood from everything below the diaphragm (legs, abdomen and pelvis) to the right atrium, entering it from below.

labels.name: Gonadal
labels.fn: The vein from each testis or ovary. The right one drains into the inferior vena cava, the left into the vein from the left kidney.

labels.name: Median cubital
labels.fn: A short superficial vein at the front of the elbow linking the cephalic and basilic veins. It is the usual vein for drawing blood, because it is large, near the surface and held in place.

follow.q: Why is the median cubital vein the usual choice for drawing blood?
options: It is wide, lies just under the skin and does not roll
It carries oxygenated blood straight from the brachial artery
It is the only vein in the arm with no valves
It is deep, so the needle is less painful
follow.why: Veins are used rather than arteries because their pressure is low. This one is wide, lies just under the skin in the antecubital area and is anchored by the tissue around it, so it is easy to find and does not roll away from the needle.

labels.name: Lumbar
labels.fn: Veins that drain the back wall of the abdomen and empty into the inferior vena cava.

labels.name: Radial
labels.fn: The deep veins that run beside the radial artery on the thumb side of the forearm.

labels.name: Median antebrachial
labels.fn: A superficial vein running up the middle of the front of the forearm, draining into the median cubital or basilic vein.

labels.name: Right and left common iliac
labels.fn: The veins formed by the external and internal iliac veins. The right and left common iliac veins join to form the inferior vena cava.

labels.name: Ulnar
labels.fn: The deep veins that run beside the ulnar artery on the little-finger side of the forearm.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The continuation of the femoral vein above the groin. It joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

labels.name: Palmar venous arches
labels.fn: Arching veins in the palm that collect blood from the fingers and pass it to the veins of the forearm.

labels.name: Internal iliac
labels.fn: The vein that drains the pelvic organs and buttocks and joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

labels.name: Deep femoral
labels.fn: The deep vein that drains the thigh muscles into the femoral vein.

labels.name: Digital
labels.fn: The small veins of the fingers or toes.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the thigh, beside the femoral artery. It continues as the external iliac vein above the groin.

labels.name: Great saphenous
labels.fn: The longest vein in the body: a superficial vein that runs from the inner foot up the inner leg and thigh to join the femoral vein in the groin. It is often used as a graft for coronary bypass surgery.

follow.q: Why do varicose veins usually appear in the superficial veins of the legs, such as the great saphenous vein?
options: Blood must rise a long way against gravity, and failed valves let it pool
They carry blood at arterial pressure, which stretches their thin walls over time
They have thicker walls than other veins
They carry blood away from the heart
follow.why: Venous valves hold up the column of blood between heartbeats. In the legs that column is tall. When valves weaken, blood falls back and pools, and the thin-walled superficial veins, with little muscle around them for support, stretch and twist.

labels.name: Popliteal
labels.fn: The deep vein behind the knee, formed by the tibial veins and joined by the small saphenous vein. It continues as the femoral vein.

labels.name: Posterior tibial
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the posterior tibial artery at the back of the leg. Calf muscle contraction squeezes them, pushing blood up toward the heart.

labels.name: Small saphenous
labels.fn: A superficial vein that runs up the back of the calf from the outer foot and drains into the popliteal vein behind the knee.

labels.name: Anterior tibial
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the anterior tibial artery at the front of the leg. They join the posterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.

labels.name: Fibular
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the fibular artery on the outer side of the leg, draining into the posterior tibial veins.

labels.name: Plantar venous arch
labels.fn: An arch of deep veins in the sole of the foot that drains into the tibial veins.

labels.name: Dorsal venous arch
accept: dorsal venous arch of the foot
labels.fn: An arch of superficial veins on the top of the foot. It gives rise to the great saphenous vein on the inner side and the small saphenous vein on the outer side.

labels.name: Superior sagittal sinus
labels.fn: A dural venous sinus along the top midline of the brain, inside a fold of the dura mater. It collects blood from the brain and also takes up cerebrospinal fluid.

labels.name: Inferior sagittal sinus
labels.fn: A small dural venous sinus in the lower edge of the fold of dura mater between the two halves of the brain. It drains into the straight sinus.

labels.name: Straight sinus
labels.fn: A dural venous sinus that runs back along the fold of dura mater, collecting blood from the inferior sagittal sinus and deep brain veins.

labels.name: Occipital
labels.fn: A vein that drains the back of the scalp.

labels.name: Temporal
labels.fn: The superficial temporal vein in front of the ear, draining the side of the scalp.

labels.name: Cavernous sinus
labels.fn: A dural venous sinus on each side of the pituitary gland. Veins from the face and eye connect with it, which is how an infection of the face can spread inside the skull.

labels.name: Right transverse sinus
labels.fn: A dural venous sinus running around the back of the skull on the right. It receives blood from the sinuses at the back of the head and continues as the sigmoid sinus.

labels.name: Maxillary
labels.fn: A deep vein of the face that drains the upper jaw region and joins the temporal vein.

labels.name: Occipital sinus
labels.fn: A small dural venous sinus at the back of the skull.

labels.name: Facial
labels.fn: The vein that drains the face, running down and back across the cheek to empty into the internal jugular vein.

labels.name: Sigmoid sinus
labels.fn: The S-shaped dural venous sinus that continues from the transverse sinus and exits the skull as the internal jugular vein.

follow.q: Blood from the dural venous sinuses leaves the skull through which vein?
follow.why: The sinuses drain toward the sigmoid sinus, which passes through the base of the skull and becomes the internal jugular vein. The external jugular drains the scalp and face from outside the skull.

labels.name: Petrosal sinus
labels.fn: A dural venous sinus along the base of the skull that drains the cavernous sinus toward the sigmoid sinus and internal jugular vein.

labels.name: External jugular
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the side of the neck that drains the scalp and face. It is often visible when a person strains or lies flat, and it empties into the subclavian vein.

labels.name: Internal jugular
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the neck, beside the common carotid artery. It drains the brain (from the dural venous sinuses), face and neck and joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.

labels.name: Vertebral
labels.fn: A vein that runs down through the neck bones beside the vertebral artery, draining the back of the neck into the brachiocephalic vein.

labels.name: Right subclavian
labels.fn: The continuation of the axillary vein under the collarbone. It drains the arm and joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. It is a common site for a central line.

labels.name: Axillary
labels.fn: The large vein of the armpit, formed by the basilic and brachial veins and joined by the cephalic vein. It becomes the subclavian vein.

labels.name: Superior vena cava
labels.fn: The large vein that returns blood from the head, neck, arms and chest to the right atrium, entering it from above.

follow.q: Blood from your right arm reaches the heart through which vessel?
follow.why: Veins above the diaphragm, including those of the arms, head and neck, drain into the superior vena cava, which opens into the right atrium. The inferior vena cava drains the body below the diaphragm.

labels.name: Subclavian
labels.fn: The continuation of the axillary vein under the collarbone. It drains the arm and joins the internal jugular vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. It is a common site for a central line.

labels.name: Axillary
labels.fn: The large vein of the armpit, formed by the basilic and brachial veins and joined by the cephalic vein. It becomes the subclavian vein.

labels.name: Cephalic
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the thumb side of the arm. It runs up to the shoulder and empties into the axillary vein, and is often used for IV lines.

labels.name: Subscapular
labels.fn: A vein that drains the back of the shoulder around the scapula into the axillary vein.

labels.name: Brachial
labels.fn: The paired deep veins that run beside the brachial artery in the upper arm and join the basilic vein to form the axillary vein.

labels.name: Basilic
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the little-finger side of the arm. It dives deep partway up the arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.

labels.name: Median cubital
labels.fn: A short superficial vein at the front of the elbow linking the cephalic and basilic veins. It is the usual vein for drawing blood, because it is large, near the surface and held in place.

follow.q: Why is the median cubital vein the usual choice for drawing blood?
options: It is wide, lies just under the skin and does not roll
It carries oxygenated blood straight from the brachial artery
It is the only vein in the arm with no valves
It is deep, so the needle is less painful
follow.why: Veins are used rather than arteries because their pressure is low. This one is wide, lies just under the skin in the antecubital area and is anchored by the tissue around it, so it is easy to find and does not roll away from the needle.

labels.name: Cephalic
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the thumb side of the arm. It runs up to the shoulder and empties into the axillary vein, and is often used for IV lines.

labels.name: Radial
labels.fn: The deep veins that run beside the radial artery on the thumb side of the forearm.

labels.name: Median antebrachial
labels.fn: A superficial vein running up the middle of the front of the forearm, draining into the median cubital or basilic vein.

labels.name: Basilic
labels.fn: A superficial vein on the little-finger side of the arm. It dives deep partway up the arm and joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.

labels.name: Ulnar
labels.fn: The deep veins that run beside the ulnar artery on the little-finger side of the forearm.

labels.name: Palmar venous arches
labels.fn: Arching veins in the palm that collect blood from the fingers and pass it to the veins of the forearm.

labels.name: Digital
labels.fn: The small veins of the fingers or toes.

labels.name: Common iliac
labels.fn: The veins formed by the external and internal iliac veins. The right and left common iliac veins join to form the inferior vena cava.

labels.name: Internal iliac
labels.fn: The vein that drains the pelvic organs and buttocks and joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The continuation of the femoral vein above the groin. It joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

labels.name: Gluteal
labels.fn: The superior and inferior gluteal veins drain the buttock muscles into the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Lateral sacral
labels.fn: Veins beside the sacrum that drain the back of the pelvis into the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Internal pudendal
labels.fn: The vein that drains the external genitals and the floor of the pelvis into the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Obturator
labels.fn: A vein that drains the inner thigh muscles and passes through the obturator foramen of the hip bone to join the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the thigh, beside the femoral artery. It continues as the external iliac vein above the groin.

labels.name: Deep femoral
labels.fn: The deep vein that drains the thigh muscles into the femoral vein.

labels.name: Femoral circumflex
labels.fn: Veins that wrap around the top of the femur and drain the hip region into the deep femoral or femoral vein.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the thigh, beside the femoral artery. It continues as the external iliac vein above the groin.

labels.name: Great saphenous
labels.fn: The longest vein in the body: a superficial vein that runs from the inner foot up the inner leg and thigh to join the femoral vein in the groin. It is often used as a graft for coronary bypass surgery.

labels.name: Popliteal
labels.fn: The deep vein behind the knee, formed by the tibial veins and joined by the small saphenous vein. It continues as the femoral vein.

labels.name: Small saphenous
labels.fn: A superficial vein that runs up the back of the calf from the outer foot and drains into the popliteal vein behind the knee.

labels.name: Anterior tibial
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the anterior tibial artery at the front of the leg. They join the posterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.

labels.name: Posterior tibial
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the posterior tibial artery at the back of the leg. Calf muscle contraction squeezes them, pushing blood up toward the heart.

labels.name: Fibular
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the fibular artery on the outer side of the leg, draining into the posterior tibial veins.

labels.name: Dorsal venous arch
accept: dorsal venous arch of the foot
labels.fn: An arch of superficial veins on the top of the foot. It gives rise to the great saphenous vein on the inner side and the small saphenous vein on the outer side.

labels.name: Digital
labels.fn: The small veins of the fingers or toes.

labels.name: External iliac
labels.fn: The continuation of the femoral vein above the groin. It joins the internal iliac vein to form the common iliac vein.

labels.name: Internal pudendal
labels.fn: The vein that drains the external genitals and the floor of the pelvis into the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Gluteal
labels.fn: The superior and inferior gluteal veins drain the buttock muscles into the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Obturator
labels.fn: A vein that drains the inner thigh muscles and passes through the obturator foramen of the hip bone to join the internal iliac vein.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the thigh, beside the femoral artery. It continues as the external iliac vein above the groin.

labels.name: Deep femoral
labels.fn: The deep vein that drains the thigh muscles into the femoral vein.

labels.name: Femoral circumflex
labels.fn: Veins that wrap around the top of the femur and drain the hip region into the deep femoral or femoral vein.

labels.name: Femoral
labels.fn: The large deep vein of the thigh, beside the femoral artery. It continues as the external iliac vein above the groin.

labels.name: Great saphenous
labels.fn: The longest vein in the body: a superficial vein that runs from the inner foot up the inner leg and thigh to join the femoral vein in the groin. It is often used as a graft for coronary bypass surgery.
