They have thicker walls than other veins
They carry blood away from the heart
follow.why: Venous valves hold up the column of blood between heartbeats. In the legs that column is tall. When valves weaken, blood falls back and pools, and the thin-walled superficial veins, with little muscle around them for support, stretch and twist.

labels.name: Popliteal
labels.fn: The deep vein behind the knee, formed by the tibial veins and joined by the small saphenous vein. It continues as the femoral vein.

labels.name: Small saphenous
labels.fn: A superficial vein that runs up the back of the calf from the outer foot and drains into the popliteal vein behind the knee.

labels.name: Anterior tibial
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the anterior tibial artery at the front of the leg. They join the posterior tibial veins to form the popliteal vein.

labels.name: Posterior tibial
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the posterior tibial artery at the back of the leg. Calf muscle contraction squeezes them, pushing blood up toward the heart.

labels.name: Fibular
labels.fn: The deep veins beside the fibular artery on the outer side of the leg, draining into the posterior tibial veins.

labels.name: Lateral plantar
labels.fn: A deep vein on the outer side of the sole that drains into the posterior tibial veins.

labels.name: Medial plantar
labels.fn: A deep vein on the inner side of the sole that drains into the posterior tibial veins.

labels.name: Plantar venous arch
labels.fn: An arch of deep veins in the sole of the foot that drains into the tibial veins.

labels.name: Hepatic portal
labels.fn: The vein formed behind the pancreas by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins. It carries blood rich in absorbed nutrients from the gut and spleen to the liver's capillaries, not to the heart.

follow.q: Blood leaving the stomach and intestines reaches which organ before it reaches the heart?
options: The liver, through the hepatic portal vein
The heart directly, through the inferior vena cava
The lungs, through the pulmonary arteries
The spleen, through the splenic vein
follow.why: A portal system joins two capillary beds in a row. Nutrients and drugs absorbed from the gut go first to the liver, which stores, converts or breaks them down; only then does the blood leave by the hepatic veins for the inferior vena cava.

labels.name: Cystic
labels.fn: The small vein of the gallbladder, which drains into the hepatic portal vein.

labels.name: Gall bladder
labels.fn: The small sac under the liver that stores and concentrates the fluid the liver makes to help digest fats. Its vein drains into the hepatic portal system.

labels.name: Right gastric
labels.fn: A vein along the lesser curve of the stomach that drains straight into the hepatic portal vein.

labels.name: Splenic
labels.fn: The vein that drains the spleen and some of the stomach and pancreas. Behind the pancreas it joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

labels.name: Superior mesenteric
labels.fn: The large vein that drains most of the gut below the stomach, beside the superior mesenteric artery. It joins the splenic vein to form the hepatic portal vein.

labels.name: Left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental)
labels.fn: The vein along the left part of the stomach's greater curve. It drains into the splenic vein. Gastroepiploic and gastro-omental are two names for the same veins.

labels.name: Right gastro-omental (gastroepiploic)
labels.fn: The vein along the right part of the stomach's greater curve. It drains into the superior mesenteric vein. Gastro-omental and gastroepiploic are two names for the same veins.

labels.name: Pancreatic
labels.fn: Small veins from the pancreas that drain into the splenic vein.

labels.name: Pancreaticoduodenal
labels.fn: Veins that drain the head of the pancreas and the first part of the gut after the stomach into the superior mesenteric or hepatic portal vein.

labels.name: Middle colic
labels.fn: A vein that drains the part of the wide gut crossing the abdomen into the superior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Inferior mesenteric
labels.fn: The vein that drains the last part of the gut, down into the pelvis. It usually empties into the splenic vein.

labels.name: Right colic
labels.fn: A vein that drains the rising part of the wide gut on the right side into the superior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Left colic
labels.fn: A vein that drains the descending part of the wide gut on the left side into the inferior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Ileocolic
labels.fn: The vein that drains the end of the narrow gut and the start of the wide gut, including the appendix, into the superior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Sigmoid
labels.fn: Veins that drain the S-shaped last loop of the wide gut into the inferior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Intestinal
labels.fn: The many veins from the long, narrow part of the gut that join to form the superior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Superior rectal
labels.fn: The vein that drains the upper end of the tract in the pelvis into the inferior mesenteric vein.

labels.name: Root
labels.fn: The top of the external nose, where it meets the forehead between the eyes.

labels.name: Bridge
labels.fn: The upper, bony part of the nose's ridge, just below the root. The nasal bones form it.

labels.name: Dorsum nasi
labels.fn: The ridge of the external nose, running from the root down to the tip.

labels.name: Ala
labels.fn: The flared wing on each side of the nose. Cartilage stiffens it, and it forms the outer wall of a nostril.

labels.name: Apex
labels.fn: The tip of the external nose.

labels.name: Philtrum
labels.fn: The vertical groove between the bottom of the nose and the upper lip. It is a landmark of the face, not part of the airway.

labels.name: Frontal bone
labels.fn: The forehead bone. Its lower edge meets the nasal bones at the root of the nose.

labels.name: Nasal bone
labels.fn: One of a pair of small bones that form the bony bridge of the nose.

labels.name: Maxillary bone
labels.fn: The upper jaw bone. Its upward process sits beside the nasal bone and frames the side of the nasal opening.

labels.name: Septal cartilage
labels.fn: The plate of hyaline cartilage that forms the front of the nasal septum, the wall between the left and right sides of the nasal cavity.

follow.q: The septal cartilage forms part of which structure?
follow.why: The septal cartilage is the front of the nasal septum, the midline wall that splits the nasal cavity into left and right halves. The conchae are shelves on the side walls, the ala is supported by the alar cartilage, and the frontal sinus is a space in the frontal bone.

labels.name: Major alar cartilage
labels.fn: The curved cartilage that shapes the tip of the nose and the ala on each side, holding the nostril open.

labels.name: Septal cartilage
labels.fn: The plate of hyaline cartilage that forms the front of the nasal septum, the wall between the left and right sides of the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Sphenoidal sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space in the sphenoid bone, behind and above the nasal cavity. Like the other paranasal sinuses, it is lined with mucous membrane and drains into the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Frontal sinus
labels.fn: An air-filled space in the frontal bone above the eyes. It drains into the nasal cavity; the sinuses make the skull lighter and add mucus and moisture to the air.

labels.name: Ethmoid bone
labels.fn: The skull bone between the eye sockets. Its thin, perforated roof plate forms the top of the nasal cavity, and the nerve fibers for smell pass up through its holes.

labels.name: Olfactory epithelium
labels.fn: The patch of epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity that holds the sensory receptors for smell.

labels.name: Nasal meatuses (superior, middle, and inferior)
labels.fn: The grooves of air space under each nasal concha. Air flowing through these narrow channels touches a large area of warm, moist lining.

labels.name: Nasal conchae
labels.fn: The three curled shelves (superior, middle and inferior) on each side wall of the nasal cavity. They make inhaled air swirl against the warm, moist mucous membrane, which warms, humidifies and cleans it.

follow.q: What do the nasal conchae do to the air you breathe in?
options: Close off the nasal cavity whenever you swallow
Hold the sensory receptors that detect smells
Make it swirl so the lining can warm and clean it
Vibrate to make the sound of the voice
follow.why: The curled conchae break the airstream into turbulent flow, so more air touches the warm, moist, mucus-covered lining, which warms it, adds water and traps particles. The smell receptors sit in the olfactory epithelium in the roof, and the voice comes from the vocal folds.

labels.name: Pharyngeal tonsil
labels.fn: Lymphoid tissue on the back wall of the nasopharynx, also called the adenoid. It traps microbes carried in with the air; when it swells in a child it can block breathing through the nose.

follow.q: A child's pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) is badly swollen. Which is it most likely to block?
follow.why: The pharyngeal tonsil sits in the nasopharynx, the air-only passage behind the nasal cavity. A swollen one blocks air coming from the nose, so the child breathes through the mouth. Food and mouth breathing use the oropharynx below it, and the glottis is in the larynx.

labels.name: Nasal vestibule
labels.fn: The skin-lined entrance just inside each nostril. Its coarse hairs filter large particles out of incoming air.

labels.name: Opening of auditory tube
labels.fn: Where the auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx. The tube links the middle ear to the throat, so air pressure on both sides of the eardrum can equalize.

labels.name: Nostril
labels.fn: One of the two openings of the nose (the nares), through which air enters the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Nasopharynx
labels.fn: The upper part of the pharynx, behind the nasal cavity. Only air passes through it, and its ciliated lining sweeps mucus down toward the throat.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: The muscular organ on the floor of the mouth. It belongs to the digestive system, but its back forms the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Palatine tonsil
labels.fn: Lymphoid tissue in each side wall of the oropharynx. It samples microbes entering through the mouth.

labels.name: Lingual tonsil
labels.fn: Lymphoid tissue at the back of the tongue, in the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. When you swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis folds down over its opening, steering food and drink toward the esophagus.

follow.q: What does the epiglottis do each time you swallow?
options: Rises to seal the nasal cavity from the throat
Folds down over the entrance to the larynx
Vibrates to make a swallowing sound
follow.why: As the larynx is pulled up during a swallow, the epiglottis tips down over its entrance, so food slides past into the esophagus instead of the airway. It does not seal the nose, make sound or work the auditory tube.

labels.name: Oropharynx
labels.fn: The middle part of the pharynx, behind the mouth. Both air and food pass through it, so it is lined with stratified squamous epithelium that stands up to rubbing.

follow.q: Why is the oropharynx lined with stratified squamous epithelium instead of a ciliated lining like the nasopharynx?
options: Oxygen must diffuse across it quickly into the blood
Swallowed food would wear a thin lining away
It makes the mucus that traps dust
It never comes into contact with air
follow.why: Food passes through the oropharynx, and many layers of flat cells can lose their surface cells to friction and still protect the tissue beneath. Gas exchange does not happen in the pharynx, the mucus comes from goblet cells and glands, and air passes through the oropharynx on every breath.

labels.name: Hyoid bone
labels.fn: The U-shaped bone in the upper neck that does not join any other bone. The larynx hangs from it, and tongue and neck muscles attach to it.

labels.name: Laryngopharynx
labels.fn: The lowest part of the pharynx, behind the larynx. It leads forward into the larynx for air and back into the esophagus for food.

labels.name: Vestibular fold
labels.fn: The upper pair of folds in the larynx, also called the false vocal cords. They do not make the voice; they help close the larynx to protect the airway.

labels.name: Thyroid cartilage
labels.fn: The largest cartilage of the larynx, a shield of hyaline cartilage in the front of the neck. Its front ridge is the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).

labels.name: Vocal fold
labels.fn: The lower pair of folds in the larynx, the true vocal cords. Air pushed out between them makes them vibrate, which produces the voice.

labels.name: Cricoid cartilage
labels.fn: The ring of hyaline cartilage at the bottom of the larynx, the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway. The trachea begins just below it.

labels.name: Nasal cavity
labels.fn: The air space inside the nose, divided into left and right by the nasal septum. Its mucous membrane warms, moistens and cleans the air you breathe in.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: The muscular organ on the floor of the mouth. It belongs to the digestive system, but its back forms the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx that folds down over the laryngeal opening during a swallow.

labels.name: Larynx (voice box)
labels.fn: The voice box: a short tube of cartilages, ligaments and membranes between the laryngopharynx and the trachea. It keeps the airway open, guards it during swallowing and makes the voice.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The muscular tube behind the trachea that carries swallowed food from the laryngopharynx to the stomach. It is part of the digestive tract, not the airway.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe, which carries air from the larynx down into the chest. It lies in front of the esophagus.

labels.name: Nasopharynx
labels.fn: The upper part of the pharynx (green here), behind the nasal cavity. Only air passes through it.

labels.name: Oropharynx
labels.fn: The middle part of the pharynx (teal here), behind the mouth. Air and food both pass through it.

labels.name: Laryngopharynx
labels.fn: The lowest part of the pharynx (purple here), behind the larynx. It opens into both the larynx and the esophagus.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. It folds down over the laryngeal opening when you swallow.

labels.name: Body of hyoid bone
labels.fn: The front, central part of the U-shaped hyoid bone. The larynx hangs from it by the thyrohyoid membrane.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of connective tissue joining the top of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid.

labels.name: Thyroid cartilage
labels.fn: The largest cartilage of the larynx: two plates of hyaline cartilage joined in front like a shield. It protects the vocal folds, which attach to its inner surface.

labels.name: Laryngeal prominence
labels.fn: The ridge at the front of the thyroid cartilage where its two plates meet, known as the Adam's apple. It is usually larger in adult men.

labels.name: Cricothyroid ligament
labels.fn: The band of connective tissue between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. It lies just under the skin, below the vocal folds.

follow.q: Something is stuck at the vocal folds and the person cannot breathe. Where can an emergency airway be opened through the front of the neck, below the blockage?
follow.why: The cricothyroid ligament lies just under the skin between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, below the level of the vocal folds, so an opening there bypasses a blockage at the glottis. The thyrohyoid membrane is above the vocal folds, the laryngeal prominence is solid cartilage, and the epiglottis is at the top of the larynx.

labels.name: Cricoid cartilage
labels.fn: The ring of hyaline cartilage at the base of the larynx. It is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, and the trachea hangs from it.

follow.q: What sets the cricoid cartilage apart from the other cartilages of the airway?
options: It vibrates to produce the sound of the voice
It is the airway's only complete ring
It is made of elastic cartilage so it can fold
It hangs directly from the body of the hyoid bone
follow.why: The cricoid is a full ring, like a signet ring with its wide part at the back, so it holds the lower larynx open all the way around. The vocal folds make the voice, the epiglottis is the elastic cartilage, and the thyroid cartilage is the one that hangs from the hyoid bone.

labels.name: Cricotracheal ligament
labels.fn: The ligament that joins the bottom of the cricoid cartilage to the top of the trachea.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The leaf-shaped flap of elastic cartilage at the top of the larynx. It folds down over the laryngeal opening when you swallow.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of connective tissue joining the top of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid.

labels.name: Body of hyoid bone
labels.fn: The front, central part of the U-shaped hyoid bone. The larynx hangs from it by the thyrohyoid membrane.

labels.name: Fatty pad
labels.fn: A pad of fat in front of the epiglottis, between it and the hyoid bone and thyrohyoid membrane. It gives the epiglottis a soft cushion to move against.

labels.name: Cuneiform cartilage
labels.fn: A small rod of elastic cartilage in the fold of tissue that runs from each arytenoid cartilage up to the epiglottis. It stiffens that fold.

labels.name: Thyrohyoid membrane
labels.fn: The sheet of connective tissue joining the top of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone. It suspends the larynx from the hyoid.

labels.name: Corniculate cartilage
labels.fn: A small horn-shaped cartilage perched on top of each arytenoid cartilage.

labels.name: Vestibular fold
labels.fn: The upper pair of folds in the larynx, the false vocal cords. They do not make the voice; they help close off the larynx.

labels.name: Arytenoid cartilage
labels.fn: One of a pair of small pyramid-shaped cartilages sitting on the back of the cricoid cartilage. The vocal folds attach to them, and muscles that swivel them open and close the gap between the folds.

follow.q: Small muscles pivot the arytenoid cartilages. What does that change?
options: The tension and spacing of the vocal folds
How far the nasal conchae stick out into the air
Where the hyoid bone sits in the neck
Whether the auditory tube is open
follow.why: The back ends of the vocal folds attach to the arytenoid cartilages, so rotating or sliding them spreads the folds apart for breathing, brings them together for speech, and changes how tight they are, which changes the pitch. The conchae, hyoid and auditory tube are not moved by these muscles.

labels.name: Vocal fold
labels.fn: The lower pair of folds in the larynx, the true vocal cords. Air pushed between them makes them vibrate and produce sound.

follow.q: You take a breath, hold it and bear down to lift something heavy. What closes the airway?
options: The vocal folds close the glottis
The epiglottis rises to seal the nose
follow.why: Muscles pull the vocal folds together so the glottis, the opening between them, is shut and air is held in the chest. The epiglottis covers the larynx during swallowing and never seals the nose, and the cricoid and thyroid cartilages are rigid.

labels.name: Thyroid cartilage
labels.fn: The largest cartilage of the larynx: two plates of hyaline cartilage joined in front like a shield. It protects the vocal folds, which attach to its inner surface.

labels.name: Cricoid cartilage
labels.fn: The ring of hyaline cartilage at the base of the larynx. It is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway, and the trachea hangs from it.

labels.name: Cricothyroid ligament
labels.fn: The band of connective tissue between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below. It lies just under the skin, below the vocal folds.

labels.name: Cricotracheal ligament
labels.fn: The ligament that joins the bottom of the cricoid cartilage to the top of the trachea.

labels.name: Pyriform fossa
labels.fn: A pocket of the laryngopharynx on each side of the larynx. Swallowed food and drink run through these pockets around the larynx on the way to the esophagus, and a fish bone can catch here.

labels.name: Esophagus
labels.fn: The entrance to the esophagus, behind the larynx. Swallowed food goes here, not into the airway.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe, seen here through the open glottis below the vocal folds.

labels.name: True vocal cord
labels.fn: The true vocal cord (vocal fold): the pale band on each side of the glottis. Air passing between the two cords makes them vibrate, producing the voice. They look white because they have few blood vessels.

follow.q: What makes the true vocal cords produce a sound?
options: Nerve signals alone, with the glottis shut
The epiglottis striking them as it folds down
Air breathed out making them vibrate
The tongue pressing on them from above
follow.why: Sound comes from air pushed up from the lungs between the nearly closed cords, which sets them vibrating. Muscles set their tension and spacing, but without airflow there is no sound. The epiglottis and tongue do not make them vibrate.

labels.name: Vestibular fold
labels.fn: The false vocal cord on each side, above the true vocal cord. It does not make the voice; it helps close off the larynx.

labels.name: Glottis
labels.fn: The vocal folds together with the opening between them. Widening it lets air through; closing it stops air, as when you hold your breath or build up pressure for a cough.

labels.name: Epiglottis
labels.fn: The epiglottis seen from above, at the front of the laryngeal opening. It folds back over the opening during swallowing.

labels.name: Tongue
labels.fn: The back of the tongue, which forms the front wall of the oropharynx.

labels.name: Nasal cavity
labels.fn: The air space inside the nose, where inhaled air is warmed, moistened and cleaned.

labels.name: Nostril
labels.fn: One of the two openings of the nose (the nares), where air enters the nasal cavity.

labels.name: Pharynx
labels.fn: The throat: a muscular tube, shared by air and food, that runs from behind the nasal cavity down to the larynx and the esophagus.

labels.name: Larynx
labels.fn: The voice box, between the pharynx and the trachea. It keeps the airway open, guards it during swallowing and makes the voice.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: a tube held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that carries air from the larynx into the chest, where it splits into the two main bronchi.

labels.name: Right main bronchus
labels.fn: The first branch of the trachea to the right lung. It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left main bronchus.

follow.q: A child breathes in a peanut. It most often lodges in the right main bronchus. Why?
options: It is wider and more vertical than the left
It has more cartilage rings, which catch objects
It is longer than the left main bronchus
The heart presses the left one shut
follow.why: The right main bronchus is wider and continues almost straight down from the trachea, so an object falling down the airway tends to follow it. The left bronchus angles off more sharply to pass beside the heart, but the heart does not close it, and cartilage rings do not catch objects.

labels.name: Left main bronchus
labels.fn: The first branch of the trachea to the left lung. It is longer, narrower and more horizontal than the right, because it runs out beside the heart.

labels.name: Right lung
labels.fn: The right lung, which has three lobes and is larger than the left.

labels.name: Left lung
labels.fn: The left lung, which has two lobes and a notch where the heart sits, so it is smaller than the right.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle under the lungs that separates the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. When it contracts it flattens, making the chest cavity larger and drawing air in.

labels.name: Trachea
labels.fn: The windpipe: a tube held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage that carries air from the larynx into the chest, where it splits into the two main bronchi.

labels.name: Superior lobe
labels.fn: The upper lobe of the left lung, separated from its inferior lobe by the oblique fissure.

labels.name: Superior lobe
labels.fn: The upper lobe of the right lung, separated from the middle lobe by the horizontal fissure.

labels.name: Main (primary) bronchus
labels.fn: A main (primary) bronchus: one of the two first branches of the trachea. Each enters its lung at the hilum.

labels.name: Lobar (secondary) bronchus
labels.fn: A lobar (secondary) bronchus: a branch of a main bronchus that supplies one lobe. The right lung has three and the left has two.

follow.q: Which airway supplies one whole lobe of a lung?
follow.why: Each main bronchus serves a whole lung and splits into lobar bronchi, one per lobe. Each lobar bronchus then splits into segmental bronchi, one per segment of the lobe, and the branching continues down to the terminal bronchioles.

labels.name: Segmental (tertiary) bronchus
labels.fn: A segmental (tertiary) bronchus: a branch of a lobar bronchus that supplies one segment of a lobe. Each segment has its own airway and blood supply.

labels.name: Middle lobe
labels.fn: The middle lobe, found only in the right lung, between its superior and inferior lobes.

follow.q: How many lobes does each lung have?
follow.why: The right lung has superior, middle and inferior lobes. The left has only superior and inferior lobes, because the heart takes up room on the left side.

labels.name: Cardiac notch
labels.fn: The indentation in the front edge of the left lung that makes room for the heart.

labels.name: Inferior lobe
labels.fn: The lower lobe of the right lung, resting on the diaphragm below the oblique fissure.

labels.name: Inferior lobe
labels.fn: The lower lobe of the left lung, resting on the diaphragm below the oblique fissure.

labels.name: Right lung
labels.fn: The right lung, which has three lobes and is larger than the left.

labels.name: Left lung
labels.fn: The left lung, which has two lobes and a notch where the heart sits, so it is smaller than the right.

labels.name: Intercostal muscle
labels.fn: The muscle between two neighboring ribs, part of the chest wall. The intercostal muscles move the ribs when you breathe.

labels.name: Lung
labels.fn: The surface of the lung, covered by the visceral pleura. Inside, the lung is spongy, filled with branching airways and tiny air sacs.

labels.name: Lung
labels.fn: The left lung, wrapped in its pleural sac. It is soft and spongy, filled with branching airways and tiny air sacs.

labels.name: Pleural sac
labels.fn: The pleura around one lung: a closed sac of serous membrane with two layers, one on the lung and one on the chest wall, and the pleural cavity between them.

labels.name: Parietal pleura
labels.fn: The outer layer of the pleura. It lines the inside of the chest wall, the top of the diaphragm and the side of the mediastinum.

labels.name: Intercostal muscles
labels.fn: The muscle between two neighboring ribs, part of the chest wall. The intercostal muscles move the ribs when you breathe.

labels.name: Visceral pleura
labels.fn: The inner layer of the pleura, stuck to the surface of the lung and dipping into its fissures.

labels.name: Pleural cavity
labels.fn: The thin space between the parietal and visceral pleura. A film of pleural fluid in it lets the layers slide and holds the lung against the chest wall.

follow.q: What does the pleural cavity of a healthy person contain?
options: Air that fills the lungs with each breath
A thin film of pleural fluid
Nothing at all, since the layers are fused
follow.why: The two pleural layers are separated only by a thin film of serous fluid. It lets them glide over each other and makes them cling together, so the lung follows the chest wall. Air in this space is abnormal, and blood stays inside vessels.

labels.name: Diaphragm
labels.fn: The dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle under the lungs that separates the thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities. When it contracts it flattens, making the chest cavity larger and drawing air in.

labels.name: Chest wall (rib cage, sternum, thoracic vertebrae, connective tissue, intercostal muscles)
labels.fn: Everything that encloses the thoracic cavity: the rib cage, sternum, thoracic vertebrae, connective tissue and intercostal muscles. The pleura links the lungs to it, so the lungs follow its movements.

labels.name: Terminal bronchiole
labels.fn: The last airway of the conducting zone. Its wall has no alveoli, so it only carries air.

labels.name: Smooth muscle
labels.fn: Bands of smooth muscle that wrap the bronchioles. Contracting narrows the airway and relaxing widens it, which changes how easily air flows.

follow.q: The smooth muscle around a bronchiole contracts. What happens to air flow through that bronchiole?
options: It rises, because the airway widens
It falls, because the airway narrows
It stays the same, since cartilage holds it open
follow.why: Contraction squeezes the bronchiole to a smaller radius, and a narrower tube resists flow much more, so less air gets through. Bronchioles have no cartilage to hold them open, which is why their smooth muscle controls their size.

labels.name: Deoxygenated blood from pulmonary artery
accept: deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery
labels.fn: A branch of the pulmonary artery bringing oxygen-poor blood from the right ventricle to the capillaries around the alveoli.

follow.q: The blood reaching the alveolar capillaries from the pulmonary artery is:
options: Oxygen-rich, from the aorta through the bronchial arteries
follow.why: The pulmonary circuit starts at the right ventricle, which pumps oxygen-poor blood returning from the body into the pulmonary trunk and arteries. The left ventricle and aorta carry oxygen-rich blood to the body, and the left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs.

labels.name: Oxygenated blood to pulmonary vein
accept: oxygenated blood to the pulmonary vein
labels.fn: A vessel carrying oxygen-rich blood away from the alveolar capillaries toward the pulmonary veins, which return it to the left atrium.

labels.name: Respiratory bronchiole
labels.fn: The first airway of the respiratory zone: a bronchiole with a few alveoli budding from its wall, so gases start to move between air and blood here.

follow.q: Where does the respiratory zone begin?
follow.why: The respiratory zone starts where alveoli first appear, in the walls of the respiratory bronchioles. Everything above that, down to and including the terminal bronchioles, is conducting zone that only moves air.

labels.name: Alveolus
labels.fn: A tiny air sac whose wall is mostly very thin type I alveolar cells, wrapped in capillaries. Oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across this thin wall.

follow.q: What makes the wall of an alveolus suited to moving gases between air and blood?
options: It is lined with a thick layer of mucus
It is stiffened by plates of cartilage
It is wrapped in bands of smooth muscle
follow.why: Diffusion is fast only over short distances, and the alveolar wall is a single layer of very flat cells pressed against capillaries. Mucus, cartilage or muscle in the way would thicken the barrier and slow diffusion.

labels.name: Alveolar sac
labels.fn: A cluster of alveoli at the end of an alveolar duct, like a bunch of grapes.

labels.name: Capillaries
labels.fn: The dense net of capillaries around the alveoli, where the blood picks up oxygen and gives up carbon dioxide.

labels.name: Alveolar duct
labels.fn: A short passage off a respiratory bronchiole whose wall is made almost entirely of alveoli. It leads to the alveolar sacs.

labels.name: Alveolar pores
labels.fn: Small openings in the walls between neighboring alveoli. They let air pass from one alveolus to the next, which evens out pressure and gives air a way around a blocked airway.

os-1-13.alt: Two views of a standing woman with paired arrows. In the side view a vertical arrow runs from cranial at the head to caudal at the lower back, and a horizontal arrow runs from posterior (dorsal) at the back to anterior (ventral) at the front. In the front view, superior is at the top of the page and inferior at the bottom, right and left are marked on her own sides, an arrow runs from the midline outward to lateral, and arrows along the left arm and right leg run from proximal near the trunk to distal at the hand and foot.

os-1-14.alt: A woman standing in anatomical position, seen from the front and slightly to one side, crossed by four flat panels. A vertical panel running front to back divides her into right and left parts (the sagittal plane). A vertical panel running side to side divides her into front and back parts (the frontal, or coronal, plane). A horizontal panel at hip level divides her into upper and lower parts (the transverse plane). A slanted panel through the lower legs is an oblique plane.

os-1-15.alt: Side and front views of the body with the cavities shaded. The cranial cavity inside the skull holds the brain, and a narrow canal runs down from it through the backbone; together they form the dorsal body cavity. In the chest, the two lung spaces sit on either side of a central space whose lower part surrounds the heart. A dome-shaped diaphragm lies below the chest. Below it, the large abdominal cavity continues into the funnel-shaped pelvic cavity; chest, abdominal and pelvic spaces together form the ventral body cavity.

os-1-17.alt: Left: the heart enclosed in a two-layered sac. The inner layer lies on the heart's surface, the outer layer forms the outside of the sac, and a thin space lies between them. Right: the same arrangement modeled by a fist pushed into a soft, partly filled balloon. The balloon wall touching the fist matches the inner layer, the far wall matches the outer layer, and the air inside matches the space between them.

os-1-12.alt: Front and back views of a person standing in anatomical position, with the surface divided into named regions: head, face, eyes, cheeks, ears, chin, neck, chest, armpit, arm, bend of the elbow, forearm, wrist, palm, fingers, abdomen, navel, hip, groin, pubic area, thigh, front of the knee, leg, ankle and foot on the front; head, neck, shoulder, back, arm, back of the elbow, lower back, sacrum, forearm, hand, buttock, thigh, back of the knee, calf, heel and sole on the back.

os-1-16.alt: Two front views of the abdomen showing the organs behind the wall. On the left, two vertical and two horizontal lines divide it into nine regions: right hypochondriac, epigastric and left hypochondriac across the top; right lumbar, umbilical and left lumbar across the middle; right iliac, hypogastric and left iliac across the bottom. On the right, one vertical and one horizontal line crossing at the navel divide it into four quadrants: right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower. The dome of the diaphragm is outlined at the top.

os-3-4.alt: A section of plasma membrane: a phospholipid bilayer with proteins spanning it or sitting on its surfaces, cholesterol tucked between the phospholipids, and sugar chains attached to some proteins and lipids on the outer face.

os-3-13.alt: A cutaway drawing of a generalized human cell showing the plasma membrane, the nucleus, and the internal structures of the cytoplasm, including the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, peroxisomes, ribosomes and a pair of centrioles.

os-3-15.alt: The Golgi apparatus drawn as a stack of flattened, curved membrane sacs, with small vesicles arriving on the side facing the endoplasmic reticulum and budding off the far side, beside an electron micrograph of the same stacked sacs.

os-3-17.alt: A peroxisome drawn as a small round sac bounded by a single membrane, with a dense, crystal-like core of enzymes inside.

os-3-18.alt: The three kinds of cytoskeleton fiber side by side: a hollow microtubule built from paired protein subunits, a thin microfilament made of two twisted strands of actin, and a rope-like intermediate filament made of many coiled protein strands.

os-4-5.alt: Close-up drawings of the membranes of two neighboring cells joined in different ways: a tight junction, where strands of protein stitch the two membranes together; a gap junction, where paired protein tubes connect the two cells' interiors; and anchoring junctions, including a desmosome with dense plaques on each side linked across the gap by adhesion proteins and anchored inside to rope-like filaments.

os-3-19.alt: Cutaway drawing of a cell nucleus. A double-layered nuclear envelope, studded with pores, surrounds the nucleus. Threads of chromatin fill the inside, and a dense, darker nucleolus sits within them. Flattened sacs of rough endoplasmic reticulum, dotted with ribosomes, curve around the outside of the envelope and connect to it.

os-3-22.alt: Levels of DNA packing, from a compact X-shaped chromosome down to its chromatin fiber, then to beads of DNA wrapped around histone proteins (nucleosomes), then to the bare double helix, and finally to the helix drawn flat as a ladder.

os-3-32.alt: A row of drawings, each with a short list of events underneath and a fluorescence micrograph below, showing a cell passing through the stages of mitosis and then cytokinesis: chromosomes condense, line up across the middle, separate to opposite ends, and two new nuclei form as the cell pinches in two.

os-4-6.alt: A grid of drawings of epithelial sheets sitting on a basement membrane. Rows are squamous (flat), cuboidal (cube-shaped) and columnar (tall) cells; columns are simple (one layer) and stratified (many layers). A separate panel shows pseudostratified columnar epithelium: one layer of cells of different heights, nuclei at different levels, cilia on top.

os-10-22.alt: A small outline of the heart with a box on its wall, enlarged into a drawing of branching, striped cardiac muscle fibers beside a capillary. Each fiber has a central nucleus, and wavy intercalated discs join the fibers end to end. A further enlargement of one disc shows desmosomes holding the two membranes together and gap junctions bridging them.

os-12-8.alt: Drawing of a single neuron. An irregular cell body holding a nucleus sends out several short, branching dendrites. One long axon leaves the cell body and is wrapped in evenly spaced segments of insulating covering; a glial cell reaches out with two arms to form two of the segments. The axon ends in many branches whose tips meet the dendrites of the next neuron. At the upper left, the axon of another neuron ends on this neuron's dendrites.

os-4-9.alt: A table of drawings of exocrine glands sunk into a surface epithelium. Each drawing shows surface cells, duct cells lining a pit, and secretory cells at its bottom. The simple glands have one unbranched duct; the compound glands have a branching duct. The secretory parts are tube-shaped (tubular), end in round sacs (alveolar, or acinar), or mix both (tubuloalveolar).

os-4-10.alt: Three drawings of a row of gland cells on a basement membrane, each with a nucleus below and a Golgi apparatus budding secretory vesicles above. Merocrine: vesicles fuse with the top of the cell and release their contents while the cell stays whole. Apocrine: the top of the cell, packed with vesicles, pinches off. Holocrine: the cell fills with product and the whole cell becomes the secretion.

os-4-4.alt: Front view of a woman's body with text boxes pointing to four kinds of membrane: the lining of the mouth and airway, the linings around the lungs and the abdominal organs, the skin of the hand, and the inside of the knee joint.

os-19-2.alt: Front view of an opened chest with the ribs cut away. The heart sits in the middle of the chest between the two lungs, resting on the dome of the diaphragm, with its pointed tip angled down and to the left. A dashed line marks the cut edge of the sac around the heart. A small side view shows the heart behind the sternum and in front of the esophagus and vertebral column.

os-19-5.alt: A small drawing of the heart with a box on its outer wall, enlarged into a slice showing the layers from inside to outside: a thin inner lining, a thick band of muscle, a thin outer covering, a narrow fluid-filled space, a thin membrane, and a tough outer fibrous layer.

os-19-6.alt: Two drawings of the outside of the heart. The front view shows the four chambers from the surface, the ear-shaped flaps of the upper chambers, the large vessels leaving the top, and surface vessels running in fat-filled grooves toward the tip. The back view shows the veins entering the upper chambers and the surface vessels on the back of the heart.

os-19-9.alt: A front view of the heart cut open in a frontal plane. It shows the two upper and two lower chambers, the wall between the lower chambers, the valves between upper and lower chambers held by thin cords to small muscles on the lower chamber walls, the valves at the exits to the two large arteries, the large veins entering, and the thick muscular wall of the lower left chamber.

os-19-12.alt: The heart seen from above with the upper chambers and large vessels removed, so all four valves are visible in one plane. Two large valves sit at the back, one with three flaps on the right side and one with two flaps on the left. Two smaller round valves with three half-moon flaps each sit in front of them.

os-19-4.alt: Two drawings of the circulation. Above, the heart with its large vessels: vessels carrying oxygen-poor blood shown in blue and vessels carrying oxygen-rich blood shown in red. Below, a loop diagram: the right side of the heart sends blood through a small loop to the capillaries of the lungs and back to the left side, which sends it through a larger loop to the capillaries of the body and back to the right side.

os-19-15.alt: Front and back views of the heart showing its own blood vessels. Red arteries branch from the base of the aorta: one runs down the front groove toward the tip, one curves around the left side in the groove between upper and lower chambers, and one runs around the right side and down the back. Blue veins run beside them and gather into a wide vein in the groove on the back of the heart that empties into the right upper chamber.

os-19-18.alt: The heart cut open in a frontal plane, seen from the front, with its conduction pathway drawn as yellow lines. A small node sits high in the wall of the right upper chamber near where the large vein from above enters. Three pathways run from it down through the right upper chamber to a second node low in the wall between the upper chambers, and a band crosses to the left upper chamber. From the second node a single bundle runs into the wall between the lower chambers, splits into right and left branches that run down toward the tip, and then fans out as fine fibers up the walls of both lower chambers.

os-20-4.alt: Three curved wedges of vessel wall side by side, each with its inner, middle and outer layers bracketed. The elastic artery has a thick middle layer packed with wavy dark elastic fibers. The muscular artery has a thick middle layer of smooth muscle, a wavy inner elastic line, and small vessels in its outer layer. The arteriole has a thin wall with only a few large smooth muscle cells in its middle layer.

os-20-5.alt: Three short capillary tubes cut open at one end. The first has an unbroken wall of endothelial cells wrapped in a complete basement membrane, with narrow clefts between cells. The second has a similar wall dotted with small pores through the cells. The third has large gaps between cells and a basement membrane with holes in it.

os-20-7.alt: Wedges of wall from three veins with their layers bracketed. The large vein has a thick outer layer containing small vessels, nerves and some smooth muscle, over a thin middle layer. The medium vein has a thin middle layer and paired flaps projecting into the lumen, shown closed, with a side view of the flaps. The venule has a very thin wall of lining cells and a trace of muscle.

os-20-24.alt: A front view of a standing woman with her main arteries drawn in red. The aorta rises from the heart, arches, and runs down the back of the trunk, giving branches to the head, both arms, the abdominal organs and the kidneys, then splits in the pelvis into two branches that run down each leg to the foot. The arm arteries divide at the elbow into two forearm branches that meet in arches in the palm.

os-20-25.alt: The aorta on its own. It rises from the aortic valve, where two small arteries leave for the heart muscle, curves up and over to the left, and runs straight down. Three branches leave the top of the curve: one short trunk on the right that splits in two, then separate branches to the left side of the neck and the left arm.

os-20-27.alt: The underside of the brain with its arteries in red. Two arteries run up the underside of the brainstem and join into one midline artery. That artery splits at its top end, and short connecting arteries link it to the two arteries arriving at the front, closing a ring of arteries around the base of the brain.

os-20-28.alt: The aorta running down the back of the chest and abdomen in front of the spine, with the ribs, diaphragm and kidneys in place. Small branches leave it in the chest for the chest wall and organs. It passes through an opening in the diaphragm, gives off a short trunk that splits three ways, single branches to the gut, paired branches to the kidneys and to the reproductive glands, and splits into two large branches in the pelvis.

os-20-11.alt: An outline drawing of a standing woman with black dots at the places where a pulse can be felt: the temple, the jaw, the side of the neck, the inner arm above the elbow, the thumb side of the wrist, the groin, the back of the knee, behind the inner ankle and on the top of the foot.

os-20-35.alt: A front view of a standing woman with her main veins drawn in blue. Veins from the head, neck and arms join into two large trunks that meet in one large vein entering the top of the heart. Veins from the legs, pelvis, kidneys and liver join a second large vein that runs up the back of the abdomen to the bottom of the heart. Superficial veins run up the inner and outer sides of each arm, and a long vein runs up the inner side of each leg.

os-20-37.alt: A side view of the head and neck showing the veins. Wide venous channels run inside the skull, along the top midline and around the back and base of the skull, and drain into a large deep vein running down the neck beside the airway. A smaller vein runs down the outside of the neck, and veins from the face and scalp join both. The neck veins end in a vein running under the collarbone.

os-20-38.alt: The veins of the right arm, front view, with deep veins shown darker than superficial ones. Deep veins run beside the forearm and arm bones. A superficial vein runs up the thumb side, another up the little-finger side, and a short vein crosses the front of the elbow to link them. All drain into a vein in the armpit and then one under the collarbone.

os-20-41.alt: The veins of the lower limb in front and back views. Deep veins run beside the leg and thigh bones and join into one vein behind the knee and one in the thigh, which passes into the pelvis. A long superficial vein runs from the inner ankle up the inner side of the leg to the groin, and a shorter one runs up the back of the calf to the back of the knee. A venous arch crosses the top of the foot.

os-20-43.alt: The abdominal organs with the veins that drain the gut. Veins from the stomach, pancreas, spleen and intestines gather into three main veins that join behind the pancreas into a single large vein running up into the liver.

os-22-3.alt: Three drawings of the nose. A front view and a side view of a face name the parts of the outer nose from the root between the eyes down the ridge to the tip and the flared wings beside each nostril. A third drawing shows the framework beneath: the nasal and upper jaw bones at the top and plates of cartilage, including the septal cartilage, forming the lower nose.

os-22-4.alt: A midline cut through the head and neck seen from the side. The nasal cavity with three curled shelves on its side wall sits above the roof of the mouth, with the sinuses of the frontal and sphenoid bones around it. Behind the nose, mouth and voice box the throat is divided into upper, middle and lower parts. The voice box below shows the leaf-shaped flap at its top, its two pairs of folds, and the large shield-shaped cartilage and ring-shaped cartilage in its wall, with the hyoid bone above.

os-22-6.alt: A side view outline of the head and neck with the throat shaded in three colors: the upper part behind the nasal cavity, the middle part behind the mouth and the lower part behind the voice box, continuing down as the esophagus behind the trachea.

os-22-7.alt: The voice box from the front and from the right side. The front view shows the U-shaped hyoid bone at the top with the leaf-shaped flap rising behind it, the large shield-shaped cartilage with a ridge in the midline, the ring-shaped cartilage below it joined by a ligament, and the rings of the windpipe beneath. The side view adds the small paired cartilages at the back and the two folds inside.

os-22-8.alt: The inside of the voice box viewed from above, looking down the throat. Two pale white bands form a V-shaped opening leading down into the windpipe; a pair of pinker folds lies above and outside them. The leaf-shaped flap sits at the front near the base of the tongue, and the opening of the esophagus lies behind.

os-22-2.alt: The upper body with the respiratory organs drawn in. Air passages run from the nostril and nasal cavity through the throat and voice box into the windpipe, which divides into a right and a left branch entering the two lungs. The right lung sits behind the ribs, and the dome-shaped diaphragm lies beneath both lungs.

os-22-13.alt: Both lungs from the front with the branching airway drawn inside. The windpipe divides into a main branch for each lung, which divides into a branch for each lobe and then smaller branches. The right lung has three lobes separated by two grooves; the left has two lobes and a hollow in its front edge where the heart sits.

os-22-14.alt: The chest from the front with the rib cage and intercostal muscles drawn on one side and a lung shown on the other, resting on the domed diaphragm. An enlarged box shows the edge of the lung: a thin membrane covering the lung, a second thin membrane lining the chest wall beside a rib and intercostal muscle, and a very narrow space between the two.

os-22-10.alt: A small airway wrapped in spiral bands of smooth muscle branches into smaller airways, the first of which have a few air sacs budding from their walls. These lead through short passages into grape-like clusters of air sacs, some cut open to show holes linking neighbors. A net of small blood vessels, blue where they arrive and red where they leave, covers one cluster.

os-12-9.alt: Three line drawings of neurons. In the first, a round cell body hangs below a single short stalk that joins one long process, which ends in branches at both ends. In the second, an oval cell body sits in the middle of a line, with one branched process leaving each end. In the third, a cell body with many short branched processes sends out one long process that ends in branches.

os-12-11.alt: A drawing of four kinds of support cells among two large branching neurons. Star-shaped cells with many branching processes sit among the neurons and touch them. Two small cells with fine, bristly processes sit nearby. A row of cube-shaped cells lines a surface at the lower left, sending long thin processes up into the tissue. Pale cells at the lower right send out arms that wrap segments of several different axons in layered sleeves.

os-12-12.alt: A drawing of a sensory neuron's round cell body covered by a layer of flattened cells, like tiles over a ball. A single stalk leaves the cell body and joins an axon that runs across the bottom of the picture. Elongated cells wrapped around the axon sit end to end along it, and the cut end of the axon shows the layers wrapped around it.

os-13-7.alt: A side view of the brain with each lobe of the cerebrum in its own color: the frontal lobe at the front, the parietal lobe on top behind it, the occipital lobe at the back and the temporal lobe along the side below. Labels mark the central sulcus between the frontal and parietal lobes, the gyri just in front of and behind it, the lateral sulcus above the temporal lobe and the parieto-occipital sulcus. The cerebellum and brainstem sit below, uncolored.

os-13-6.alt: Two drawings of the whole brain. The side view shows the folded surface of the cerebrum, its outer layer, and a dotted outline marking where the band of fibers joining the two halves lies deep inside. The front view shows the right and left halves of the cerebrum separated by a deep groove down the midline, with the brainstem below.

os-13-11.alt: The right half of the brain seen from the midline cut. Near the center, the egg-shaped thalamus is shaded green, the hypothalamus below and in front of it is shaded orange, and the pituitary gland hangs from the bottom of the hypothalamus on a short stalk.

os-13-12.alt: The right half of the brain seen from the midline cut, with the brainstem colored in three parts: the midbrain at the top, the rounded, bulging pons in the middle, and the medulla at the bottom, where the brainstem narrows to continue as the spinal cord.

os-15-12.alt: The brain cut down the midline with a head outline. A ring of colored structures around the center makes up the limbic system: the cingulate gyrus arching above the band of fibers joining the hemispheres, the hippocampus curving along the bottom, the almond-shaped amygdala at its front tip, and nuclei of the hypothalamus. The thalamus sits in the middle of the ring.

os-13-13.alt: Two views of the cerebellum. The top line drawing shows the cerebellum cut down the middle behind the brainstem: branching white matter inside, called the arbor vitae, spreads like a tree into folds of gray matter. The pons and an olive-shaped bulge on the medulla are labeled in front of it. Below, a brain scan cut down the midline shows the cerebellum shaded purple at the back and bottom of the skull.

os-13-17.alt: A cut through the top of the head across the midline groove between the hemispheres. From outside in: bone; the thick, two-layered dura mater, which splits in the midline to enclose a large triangular venous channel; the thin arachnoid mater; a space crossed by fine strands; and the pia mater on the folded cortex. Rounded knobs of arachnoid push up through the dura into the venous channel. Veins from the brain surface cross the layers to reach it.

os-13-18.alt: The brain and upper spinal cord cut down the midline, with the fluid spaces shaded blue. A C-shaped chamber in the hemisphere connects through a small opening to a narrow midline chamber, then a thin canal through the midbrain leads to a chamber between the brainstem and the cerebellum. Tufts of tissue lie in the chambers. Arrows show fluid leaving the lower chamber through openings, flowing around the brain and down around the spinal cord, and entering a large venous channel at the top of the head through knobs of the arachnoid. The spinal cord has a thin central canal.

os-13-23.alt: The underside of the brain, with the frontal lobes at the top and the brainstem and cerebellum at the bottom. Twelve pairs of nerve roots are highlighted. Two slender bulb-tipped nerves lie under the frontal lobes, an X-shaped crossing of two thick nerves sits behind them, and the remaining roots emerge in order down the midbrain, pons and medulla, the last ones as rows of small rootlets along the medulla and a long root running up beside it.

os-13-24.alt: An outline of the trunk and pelvis showing the spinal cord and the numbered spinal nerves on both sides, from C1 at the neck to S5 at the sacrum. Brackets group the nerves into four networks: C1 to C4 in the neck, C5 to T1 at the shoulder, L1 to L4 in the lower back and L5 to S5 in the pelvis. On one side, nerves leave the neck network toward the diaphragm, five nerves leave the shoulder network toward the arm, and nerves leave the lower networks for the front of the thigh and, as one thick nerve that splits in two, the back of the thigh.
